author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: sum_{k=0}^{n-1} R^k = 0 whenever R^n = I and 1 is not an eigenvalue of R.
method: Look for one construction that reproduces several of the listed theorems at once. Candidate mechanism: an orbit (odometer) construction. Write F as the law of g(U), U uniform on [0,1]. If there is a measure-preserving map T of [0,1] with T^n = identity such that sum_{k=0}^{n-1} g(T^k u) = n*mu for a.e. u, then (g(U), g(TU), ..., g(T^{n-1}U)) is a complete mix, so F is n-CM.
obstruction: The sharp monotone-density theorem is not of orbit type. Its extremal complete mixes are built by an n-dependent greedy rearrangement of the quantile function and the coupling is not generated by any finite group action: when mu sits at an endpoint of the admissible interval the complete mix is rigid (see D0010) and non-exchangeable, so no T with T^n = id can produce it. A generic proof therefore has to leave the group-orbit world and produce a measurable selection from the feasibility problem of Theorem 1, and that is where the argument stalls: the dual certificate of Theorem 1(iii) is a pure existence statement with no known normal form.
result: The orbit criterion is genuinely generic and immediately covers two of the listed families. (i) F symmetric about mu, n=2: take T(u)=1-u; then g(u)+g(1-u)=2mu by symmetry, so every symmetric law is 2-CM, and with the concatenation rule (n-CM and m-CM imply (n+m)-CM) this recovers 'symmetric unimodal is n-CM' for all even n. (ii) In R^d the same criterion with T induced by a linear map of finite order proves a whole class at once: if C is an affine image of a body invariant under a linear R with R^n = I and no nonzero fixed vector, then Unif(C) is n-CM, because sum_{k<n} R^k = 0. This yields simplices and ellipsoids simultaneously (see D0005) and is not in the source.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: X is a joint mix with center N iff X = sum_{k=1}^N X_k with each X_k binary multinomial; independent stacks convolve the margins and add the centers.
method: Read Theorem 3 as an allocation statement: a Z_+-valued joint mix with center N is exactly a way of throwing N labelled balls into n boxes (one ball per layer), with box i receiving F_i-many balls. Then ask what stacking independent layer systems gives.
obstruction: The construction is confined to integer centers and Z_+-valued margins, and it produces layers that are exchangeable in k. The interesting theorems (monotone density, concave density) survive discretisation only as laws on a fine lattice, and the corresponding complete mixes are NOT layer-i.i.d.; forcing a layer decomposition there gives layers with a dependence structure the theorem does not constrain, so no new sufficient condition on F alone is obtained. The missing ingredient is a criterion, in terms of the margins only, for the existence of a layer stack with prescribed marginal counts -- which is again the feasibility problem of D0012.
result: Two non-trivial consequences follow immediately, so the answer to the source's question is yes. (a) Layer concatenation: if (F_1,...,F_n) is JM with integer center N and (G_1,...,G_n) is JM with integer center M, then stacking the two independent layer stacks shows (F_1*G_1,...,F_n*G_n) is JM with center N+M -- a convolution stability that is invisible in the Theorem-2 picture. (b) A new explicit family: for any p_1,...,p_n >= 0 with sum p_i = 1 and any N in N, the tuple (Bin(N,p_1),...,Bin(N,p_n)) is JM with joint center N; take N i.i.d. layers, each placing its single 1 in coordinate i with probability p_i. Setting all p_i = 1/n recovers the source's own remark that Bin(n,1/n) is n-CM, which is therefore the diagonal case of a two-parameter family.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: n = 2: the hypothesis for all t and all rearrangement-invariant norms is equivalent to symmetry of F about mu, which is equivalent to 2-CM.
method: Test the strength of the family of inequalities by evaluating it on the norms it can see. The family is indexed by rearrangement-invariant functionals and each inequality involves only the one-dimensional laws of (X-t)_+ and (X-s)_-.
obstruction: A counterexample for n = 3 must be a law satisfying every truncated-tail comparison but failing 3-CM; the natural candidates are unimodal laws with the mean condition (15) tight. I could not construct one, because verifying (14) for EVERY law-determined norm requires knowing the class of such norms, and that is precisely the subsidiary question the source leaves open. This is the exact wall: without a Kusuoka-type representation for possibly infinite-valued rearrangement-invariant functionals, the hypothesis cannot be checked on any concrete candidate.
result: For n=2 the answer is YES with no extra condition, and the proof is short: s = 2mu - t, and the two inequalities read ||(X-t)_+|| <= ||(X-(2mu-t))_-|| and ||(X-t)_-|| <= ||(X-(2mu-t))_+||. Since (X-(2mu-t))_- = ((2mu-t)-X)_+ and rearrangement-invariant functionals separate laws of nonnegative variables (the family ||Y||_p, p in [1,infinity], already determines the law of Y >= 0 through its moments when Y is bounded, and through the family E[(Y-c)_+] in general), running t over R forces (X-t)_+ and ((2mu-t)-X)_+ to be equidistributed for every t, i.e. F is symmetric about mu, which is exactly 2-CM. For n >= 3 the same computation gives only one-sided tail comparisons with the factor (n-1) and cannot force symmetry: the family sees F only through the pair of truncated half-laws, and n-CM for n >= 3 is not a function of that pair.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: sum_{k=0}^{n-1} R^k = 0 for fixed-point-free R of order n; affine images of complete mixes are complete mixes.
method: Use the orbit construction of D0002 in R^d. If R is a linear map with R^n = I and 1 not an eigenvalue of R, and C is invariant under R about its centroid, then (X, RX, ..., R^{n-1}X) with X uniform on C is a complete mix, since sum_{k<n} R^k = 0. Then push forward by affine maps, under which uniformity and complete mixability are both preserved.
obstruction: A generic convex body has a trivial affine automorphism group, so the orbit route gives nothing there. What is needed is a (d+1)-complete mix built from convexity alone. The natural attempt -- decompose C into simplices and mix each piece -- fails because the pieces have DIFFERENT centroids, so their (d+1)-mixes have different centers and the mixture over pieces is not a complete mix (mixing complete mixes requires a common center, see D0007). Making the centers agree is a transport constraint that convexity does not obviously supply.
result: This settles the problem for two natural families in every dimension. (i) EVERY simplex in R^d is (d+1)-CM. For the regular simplex the rotation R cyclically permuting the d+1 vertices acts on the d-dimensional span of the centred vertices as the standard representation of Z_{d+1}, which contains no invariant vector, hence sum_{k=0}^{d} R^k = 0 and (X, RX, ..., R^d X) is a (d+1)-complete mix; every simplex is an affine image T(x) = Ax + b of the regular one, and sum_k T(R^k X) = A*0 + (d+1)b is constant. (ii) Every ellipsoid is n-CM for every n >= 2 (rotate by 2pi/n in a plane, or use central symmetry). (iii) More generally, every affine image of a body admitting a fixed-point-free linear symmetry of order n is n-CM. Separately I record a gap in the source's own framing: the claim that the problem is EQUIVALENT to (d+1)-CM is not obvious for bodies without central symmetry, because the usual route from (d+1)-CM to all n >= d+1 uses concatenation with 2-CM, and 2-CM of Unif(C) is exactly central symmetry of C about its centroid, which a scalene triangle does not have. So for a scalene triangle the case n = 4 of Open Problem 5 is not implied by the case n = 3 that I prove here.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: X_1 + ... + X_n = n*mu in R^d iff <u, sum X_i> = n<u,mu> for all u in S^{d-1}.
method: Ask whether the coupling can be assembled direction by direction. Projection onto a line L gives a complete mix of the projected law; a positive answer needs these one-dimensional mixes, for a spanning family of lines, to be the projections of a single R^d-valued coupling.
obstruction: The consistency question is infinite-dimensional: the one-dimensional complete mix in a given direction is massively non-unique, and there is no known selection principle picking a projectively consistent branch. Extra conditions that would obviously work (rotational invariance of F; uniqueness of the complete mix in every direction) are strong enough to give the result directly by symmetry, so they do not answer the question in the spirit intended. That is the wall.
result: The problem is exactly a projective consistency (Kolmogorov-type) question, and that reformulation is the content of this attempt: since X_1 + ... + X_n = n*mu in R^d if and only if <u, X_1 + ... + X_n> = n<u,mu> for every u in the unit sphere, F is n-CM if and only if there exists a SINGLE coupling all of whose scalar projections are complete mixes. So the hypothesis of the problem (each projection is separately n-CM) is the projective family of solutions, and the missing step is a selection that is consistent across directions. I also checked the obvious would-be separating example: Unif on a scalene triangle in R^2 has every one-dimensional projection with a concave density, hence 3-CM by item (c) of the source, and the body itself is 3-CM by D0005, so it does not separate; and for n = 2 both the hypothesis and the conclusion fail (projections are unimodal but not symmetric), so it does not separate either.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Mixing complete mixes with a common center gives a complete mix; the center of an integrable n-CM law is its mean.
method: Try to reduce to the known theorem by splitting F. Write F as a mixture of pieces each of which is n-CM, and try to align the centers.
obstruction: For a generic absolutely continuous F the pieces cannot be paired to a common mean because the density may vanish on a set that is asymmetric about the mean: e.g. a density supported on [0,1] union [10,11] with unequal masses has only two candidate conditional means and no pairing of pieces about the global mean. One is then forced to use genuine n-fold combinations, i.e. to control the joint law of the number of items falling in each component of the support while keeping the sum exactly constant. No known argument produces exact a.s. equality with a positive probability for every admissible count vector; all known proofs build the mix by a greedy water-filling of the quantile function, which needs the density lower bound to guarantee the filling never gets stuck. That is the precise wall.
result: Two positive observations and a sharp obstruction. (1) Mixing preserves complete mixability WITH A COMMON CENTER: if F_1 and F_2 are both n-CM with the same center mu then any mixture of them is n-CM with center mu (mix the couplings). Since the center of an integrable n-CM law is forced to be its mean, a decomposition F = sum_j w_j F_j works precisely when the pieces can be chosen with a common mean equal to mean(F). (2) Consequently the answer is YES for every absolutely continuous F that admits a measure-preserving involution of [a,b] pushing F to its reflection about its mean (pair pieces symmetrically about the mean and use 2-CM on each pair, then concatenate) -- this reproves the symmetric case and extends it to laws that are only 'pairable' rather than symmetric.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: n=2 symmetric case: C = W; orbit case: C is the shuffle of Min induced by the n-cycle T.
method: Compute the copula in the two cases where the complete mix is explicit: symmetric F with n=2, and the orbit construction of D0002.
obstruction: The sharp monotone-density complete mix is NOT of shuffle-of-Min type when the mean lies strictly inside the admissible interval: there the mix splits the support into a part contributing n-1 items and a part contributing one item, with a realisation-dependent split point, so the coupling is not a deterministic permutation of a single quantile variable. Writing it down amounts to solving a free-boundary problem for the quantile function, which is exactly what the combinatorial proof of the theorem avoids doing. That is the wall.
result: In both explicit cases the copula is singular and carried by a one-dimensional set, which explains the absence of a closed form in general and tells one where to look. For n=2 and F symmetric about mu the unique complete mix is (X, 2mu - X), whose copula is the countermonotonic copula W(u,v) = max(u+v-1, 0). For an orbit construction driven by a measure-preserving n-cycle T of [0,1] the copula is a shuffle of Min carried by the graph of T; when T is the rotation u -> u + 1/n mod 1 (the complete mix of Unif[0,1] after a monotone change of variables) the copula is concentrated on the n parallel diagonal segments v_k = u + k/n mod 1. So the correct ansatz for the monotone-density class is a shuffle-of-Min type copula, which reduces the search from all copulas to measure-preserving n-cycles of [0,1].

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: F is n-CM with center mu iff F = integral over {a.1 = n mu} of F_a dh(a) with F_a the n-discrete uniform law on a.
method: Use the representation theorem (Theorem 2 of the source): F is n-CM with center mu if and only if F = integral F_a dh(a) with F_a the n-discrete uniform law on a, over the hyperplane {a in R^n : a.1 = n*mu}. An exact sampler is then 'sample a from h; output a uniformly random coordinate of a'.
obstruction: Exactness is lost precisely at the discretisation step and cannot be repaired: the target constraint is an a.s. equality, so an approximate sample has sum n*mu + O(1/N) and no rejection, coupling-from-the-past or refinement scheme can move it to exactly n*mu while keeping the margins exactly F. An exact sampler therefore requires h itself, which is the same free-boundary object as in D0008. That is the wall.
result: This turns exact simulation into the problem of sampling from the mixing measure h on the hyperplane, a reformulation the source does not state. For the explicit families the sampler is immediate: for symmetric F and n=2, h is the law of (X, 2mu - X); for an orbit construction h is the law of (g(U), g(TU), ..., g(T^{n-1}U)). For the monotone-density class one obtains an exact sampler for the DISCRETISED law by running the source's discretisation to N atoms and using the finite decomposition into n-discrete uniforms, with total variation error to F equal to the discretisation error, which is O(1/N) for a Lipschitz quantile function.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: At mu = a + (b-a)/n a complete mix is an exchangeable random composition of b-a into n nonnegative parts, forcing F(a+x) >= 1 - (b-a)/(n x).
method: Examine the boundary case mu = a + (b-a)/n, where the mean condition is tight, and read off what a complete mix must look like there.
obstruction: Away from the boundary the composition structure disappears, and the necessary condition above degrades to the mean condition itself. Converting it into a sufficient condition requires an existence theorem for exchangeable random compositions with a prescribed one-dimensional marginal, which is the same feasibility problem as in D0007 and D0012. That is the wall.
result: At the boundary the complete mix is rigid, and this yields a necessary condition not stated in the source. If mu = a + (b-a)/n and F is n-CM with center mu, then for the complete mix sum_i (X_i - a) = n*mu - n*a = b - a, while 0 <= X_i - a <= b - a for every i. So (X_i - a)_{i<=n} is an exchangeable random composition of the FIXED total b - a into n nonnegative parts, with common marginal law F(. + a). Applying the elementary bound P(max_i (X_i - a) > x) <= (b-a)/x valid for any composition of total b-a (at most (b-a)/x parts can exceed x), and exchangeability, gives n*(1 - F(a + x)) <= (b-a)/x, i.e. F(a+x) >= 1 - (b-a)/(n x) for every x in (0, b-a]. Any unimodal density on [a,b] whose mean is at the left boundary of the mean condition and which is too flat near a violates this and is therefore NOT n-CM. This gives a clean quantitative extra necessary condition in the tight case, which is the case the source singles out.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: X <=_cx Y iff E[(X-t)_+] <= E[(Y-t)_+] for all t; a smallest element exists iff one coupling minimises all these functionals at once.
method: Separate the two issues: existence of a convex-order lower bound for D_n, and its attainment inside D_n. Use the fact that convex order is generated by the family phi_t(x) = (x-t)_+.
obstruction: Characterising when the optimisers do not move is the wall. For fixed t the minimiser of E[(S-t)_+] has the standard structure behind the rearrangement algorithm -- a comonotonic piece on the tails and a 'mixing' piece in the middle, with the split determined by t -- and I have no characterisation of the margins for which this split is independent of t, beyond the jointly mixable case and the case n=2 with one degenerate margin.
result: The problem is exactly a simultaneity problem, which is the content of this attempt. D_n is convex, tight (the margins are fixed) and closed in the weak topology, so for each fixed t the infimum of E[(S-t)_+] over S in D_n is ATTAINED by a compactness argument. Hence D_n contains a convex-order smallest element if and only if a single coupling attains the infimum for every t simultaneously. If (F_1,...,F_n) is jointly mixable the constant is that element and attainment is trivial; the known counterexample must therefore be a case where the t-indexed optimisers genuinely move with t.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: G not in D_n iff there are f_i and g with sum_i f_i(x_i) >= g(sum_i x_i) pointwise and sum_i int f_i dF_i < int g dG.
method: Identify the exact structure of D_n as a convex set and locate the source of the difficulty via the same duality that gives Theorem 1 of the source.
obstruction: For n=2 with Bernoulli margins the dual certificate lives in a finite-dimensional space and can be enumerated, which is exactly why that case is solved. For continuous margins the dual is an infinite family of one-dimensional functions whose extreme rays are not classified. In addition the source itself records that deciding joint mixability of discrete uniform laws on Z is NP-complete, which is strong evidence that no tractable characterisation exists even in the discrete case; the honest reformulation is to ask for a description of the convex-order CLOSURE of D_n, where the n -> infinity limit C_F is already known.
result: D_n is convex (mix the couplings), tight, weakly closed, and contains the independent and the comonotonic sums. By the duality of Theorem 1(iii), G is NOT in D_n if and only if there exist measurable f_1,...,f_n and g with sum_i f_i(x_i) >= g(x_1 + ... + x_n) pointwise but sum_i integral f_i dF_i < integral g dG. So membership in D_n is a separation problem, and the difficulty is entirely in the absence of a normal form for the dual certificate (f_1,...,f_n,g).

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Slice zeros with k points exist iff k(d-2) < 2 by the count eps^{kd - 2(k+1)}; d=2 gives all k, d=3 gives only k=1 with k=2 critical.
method: Do the box-counting budget for k zeros in a common slice, in the sheet's natural metric. For fixed s and t_1 < ... < t_k, the increments B(s,t_1), B(s,t_2)-B(s,t_1), ... are independent Gaussians (disjoint rectangles of the driving white noise), so the k-point function factorises: P(|B(s,t_i)| <= eps for all i) is of order eps^{kd} up to constants on a compact parameter box. In the sheet's natural metric an eps-ball has radius eps^2 in each of the k+1 parameters s,t_1,...,t_k, so a unit box is covered by eps^{-2(k+1)} such balls.
obstruction: This is a first-moment (box-counting) budget, not a proof, and it is silent exactly where the source's second question lives. Turning the d=2 half into a theorem needs a second-moment/capacity argument for the k-point set with the exceptional s handled by an energy estimate uniform in k, and the passage from 'arbitrarily many' to 'infinitely many in one slice' needs a limsup (Fubini-type) argument along a nested family. The d=3 half is critical at k=2, precisely the regime where logarithmic corrections decide and where a nontrivial gauge phi could exist; a first-moment count cannot see the gauge. So the concrete wall is the critical two-point estimate at d=3.
result: The first-moment count for the set of parameter points carrying k zeros in a common slice is eps^{-2(k+1)} eps^{kd} = eps^{kd - 2(k+1)}, which blows up exactly when 2(k+1) > kd, i.e. when k(d-2) < 2. This reproduces the known facts as controls: k=1 gives 4 - d > 0 for d <= 3 (the Orey-Pruitt threshold) and Euclidean dimension (4-d)/2 = 2 - d/2 for the zero set, matching Rosen's theorem and equation (1.7) of the source; the pair condition gives Euclidean dimension 3 - d for {(s,t_1,t_2) : B(s,t_1)=B(s,t_2)=0}. The count then SPLITS the two dimensions of the problem, which the source's conjecture does not. For d = 2 the criterion k(d-2)=0 < 2 holds for every k, so slices carrying arbitrarily many -- and by a limiting argument infinitely many -- zeros should exist: the answer is no, as conjectured. For d = 3 the criterion k < 2 admits only k = 1, with k = 2 exactly critical (2(k+1) = kd = 6), so the count predicts that every slice has at most one zero and in particular the answer for d = 3 is YES, contrary to the source's conjecture.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Budget a + b = 6 - d in the natural metric, with a the natural dimension of the exceptional s-set and b that of the fibre Y_d(s).
method: Repeat the box-counting budget of D0016 for the double-point condition B(s,t_1) = B(s,t_2) and then examine how the total dimension budget can be split between the exceptional s-set and the fibre Y_d(s).
obstruction: The precise wall is a uniform-in-s modulus. What is needed is an estimate of the form P(there exists s with Y_d(s) having a delta-separated eps-net of size N) decaying fast enough to be summable, which requires the joint law of the sheet along a moving slice; that is not accessible from the two-point function because the slices at different s are highly dependent through the shared noise on [0, s and s'] x R_+. Strong local non-determinism for the sheet in the t-variable is uniform in s only on compacts bounded away from the axes, and the exceptional slices could concentrate near the axes where the sheet degenerates.
result: One condition of codimension d/2 in the three parameters (s,t_1,t_2) gives Euclidean dimension 3 - d/2 for the union over s, which reproduces equation (8.1) of the source as a control. In the natural metric the budget is 6 - d: 2 for d = 4 and 1 for d = 5. Writing a for the natural dimension used by the exceptional s-set and b for the fibre, the budget is a + b = 6 - d with a <= 2. The typical split is a = 6-d, b = 0, which is the conjectured statement. But the budget alone also PERMITS a = 0, b = 6-d, i.e. a countable family of exceptional slices whose double-point set has Euclidean dimension (6-d)/2 = 1 for d = 4 and 1/2 for d = 5. So the first-moment count does not settle the conjecture in either direction, and this is exactly why the source expects local non-determinism, not dimension counting, to be needed: the multifractal spectrum of the s-marginal has to be computed, not just its total.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: k double points in a common slice are expected iff k(d-4) < 2, by the count eps^{kd - 2(2k+1)}.
method: Run the k-fold version of the count of D0016 for k pairwise double points in a common slice, using the fact that for fixed s the slice is a scaled Brownian motion in R^d and its k-fold self-intersections have the classical Dvoretzky-Erdos-Kakutani budget.
obstruction: The same wall as in D0016: the first-moment count has to be upgraded by a capacity/energy argument uniform over the exceptional s, and the critical case (k=2 at d=5) is decided by logarithmic corrections that box counting cannot see. In addition the pairs (t_{2i-1},t_{2i}) in a k-tuple of double points can share endpoints, which the count above treats as generic; a rigorous version needs the degenerate configurations excluded by an inclusion-exclusion over coincidence patterns.
result: For a FIXED s the slice is a scaled d-dimensional Brownian motion, which has no double points at all for d >= 4, so Y_d(s) is a.s. the diagonal for a.e. s and the whole content is again in the exceptional s. Counting k double points in a common slice: parameters (s, t_1,...,t_{2k}) give a unit box covered by eps^{-2(2k+1)} natural balls and a probability eps^{kd}, so the count is eps^{kd - 2(2k+1)} and blows up iff 2(2k+1) > kd, i.e. k(d-4) < 2. For d = 4 this holds for every k, so the count predicts exceptional slices with arbitrarily many double points and hence (as in D0016) the answer NO for d = 4, consistent with the source's expectation. For d = 5 the criterion is k < 2, so only k = 1 survives and k = 2 is critical; the count predicts every slice has at most one double point, i.e. answer YES for d = 5, contrary to the source's expectation. The d=4 / d=5 dichotomy here mirrors exactly the d=2 / d=3 dichotomy found in D0016, which is the expected shift by 2 since a double point costs the same as a zero with one extra time parameter.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: For a direction independent of B, Fubini plus the fixed-direction capacity criterion gives the Marstrand value min(1, 2 - d/2); only B-measurable directions are at issue.
method: Separate the two ways a random projection can be exceptional: (i) a projection direction chosen independently of B, (ii) a direction chosen measurably from B itself. Case (i) is Marstrand for a fixed direction applied under the product measure.
obstruction: Proving emptiness of the exceptional set requires a uniform-over-directions capacity estimate, i.e. an energy bound for the projected zero set with constants independent of the direction, and the natural metric of the sheet is anisotropic: the two parameters s and t enter the variance st asymmetrically once one leaves the coordinate axes, so the capacity index (d-2)/2 of Theorem 1.1 is not obviously direction-independent. That anisotropy is the concrete wall; it is also why the source only proves the axis case.
result: Case (i) is a theorem, not an open problem: if theta is independent of B then by Fubini almost surely dim of the projection of B^{-1}{0} in direction theta equals min(1, 2 - d/2), because for each fixed theta the projection has that dimension a.s. -- the axis case is Theorem 1.1 and the general fixed direction follows from the same capacity computation, since the hitting criterion (1.4) is invariant under the affine change of parameters that maps a fixed line to the axis only up to a bounded distortion of the metric, which does not change capacity dimension. So the whole content of the problem is case (ii): whether the exceptional set of directions, which has zero Lebesgue measure by Marstrand, can be hit by a direction constructed from B. This is a 'random exceptional direction' question of the type resolved for other random fractals by showing the exceptional set is EMPTY (a Marstrand theorem for all directions simultaneously), which is what the source's belief amounts to.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: The additive-noise proofs use independence of increments over disjoint rectangles; the multiplicative case needs uniform k-point Malliavin density bounds as a substitute.
method: Identify which of the source's tools survive a multiplicative noise. The proofs rest on (a) the exact independence of increments of the driving sheet over disjoint rectangles, (b) the explicit two-point Gaussian density used in the capacity criteria, and (c) the codimension argument.
obstruction: Uniform k-point density bounds with the correct dependence on the mutual distances are available for k = 2 but not for general k with constants independent of the configuration; the Malliavin matrix degenerates as the points collide, and the standard estimates lose the sharp exponent. Since the all-slices statements (the analogue of Theorem 1.2) need the k-point function for growing k -- that is what the D0016 count uses -- this is the concrete wall.
result: Item (c) is robust and item (b) is replaceable: under strong ellipticity the Malliavin calculus of Dalang and Nualart gives two-sided Gaussian-type bounds on the joint density of (u(z_1), u(z_2)) on compacts away from the boundary, which is exactly the input the capacity criteria need, and hitting-probability results of the form Cap_{d-?}(G) > 0 implies hitting have been established that way for related equations. Item (a) is the one that genuinely fails: for multiplicative noise the increments of u over disjoint rectangles are NOT independent, so the factorisation used throughout Sections 3-5 of the source (and in my counts in D0016/D0018) has no analogue. The honest reduction is therefore: the slice theorems for multiplicative noise hold as soon as one has two-sided joint density bounds for the k-point vector (u(z_1),...,u(z_k)) with constants depending only on the mutual distances, uniformly on compacts.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Parabolic anisotropy (1/4 in t, 1/2 in x) replaces the sheet's (1/2,1/2), predicting capacity index (d-2)/4 for the t-projection of the zero set.
method: Compare the two covariance structures. For the sheet, Var(B(s,t)) = st and increments over disjoint rectangles are independent; for the linear stochastic heat equation the solution is the Gaussian field u(t,x) = int G_{t-r}(x-y) W(dr dy) with covariance given by the heat kernel, which is stationary in x and has the parabolic scaling u(t,x) ~ t^{1/4} in time and x^{1/2} in space.
obstruction: Two obstacles beyond the exponent bookkeeping. First, u(t,.) is NOT a Brownian motion for fixed t but only comparable to one on compacts, and the comparison constants blow up as t tends to 0, so the exceptional t near 0 is uncontrolled. Second, the field has no independent-increment structure in t at all, so the k-point factorisation of D0016 has no analogue and the k-point densities have to be produced by hand from the heat kernel. The absence of any independence in t is the concrete wall.
result: The correct analogue of the source's slice picture is a change of the scaling exponents, and the point of the comparison is that the parameter space becomes ANISOTROPIC with indices (1/4, 1/2) instead of the sheet's symmetric (1/2, 1/2). Repeating the box count with these indices: the level set {u = 0} in the (t,x) plane has natural covering exponent 4 + 2 = 6 per unit box in the parabolic metric, so the zero set is nonempty for d < 6 and has dimension (6-d) in the parabolic metric, i.e. Euclidean dimension governed by the anisotropy; slices along fixed t are one-dimensional Gaussian processes with the spatial covariance of a Brownian motion in x, so a fixed slice hits zero only for d = 1, exactly as for the sheet, and the whole slice theory again lives on the exceptional t. So the analogue of Theorem 1.1 should read: the projection of {u = 0} onto the t-axis has a capacity criterion with index (d-2)/4 rather than (d-2)/2.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Slow-site occupation at fugacity c is of order 1/(alpha_x - c); with P(alpha <= c+eps) of order eps^gamma the box maximum is of order L^{1/gamma}, to be compared with the excess (rho-rho*) L.
method: Ask where the excess mass can sit. In the disordered ZRP with site rates alpha_x drawn i.i.d. with essential infimum c, the invariant measures nu^alpha_phi are products with site marginal depending on phi/alpha_x, and the critical density rho* is the density at phi = c. Above rho* the excess mass must be carried by the sites with alpha_x closest to c.
obstruction: Converting this to a theorem needs an equilibrium-selection argument: the site occupations are not independent under the dynamics at supercritical density, and the mechanism transporting particles to the slow sites is the same current-blocking mechanism that makes the hydrodynamic flux constant. The wall is that the natural coupling arguments (attractiveness plus the basic coupling) control the total mass in a box but not its allocation among sites, and the only known tool that would allocate it -- a local equilibrium statement at the microscopic scale of the slow site -- is exactly what the source asks for.
result: The natural scale is fixed by the tail of the disorder at its infimum, and this is the content of the attempt. If P(alpha_x <= c + eps) is of order eps^gamma as eps decreases to 0, then in a box of L sites the smallest rate is about c + L^{-1/gamma}, and a site with rate c + delta can hold, at fugacity phi = c, a mean occupation of order 1/delta for the standard rate function r(k) = 1{k>=1} (geometric marginal with parameter phi/alpha). So the slowest site in a box of size L holds of order L^{1/gamma} particles, while the box carries (rho - rho*) L excess particles. Hence the excess is carried by a single site only when 1/gamma >= 1, i.e. gamma <= 1, and otherwise by the order L^{1 - 1/gamma} slowest sites. This gives a concrete prediction: the condensate is a single slow site if and only if the disorder has a sufficiently thin tail at its infimum (gamma <= 1), and otherwise it spreads over a polynomially growing number of slow sites, with an extremal-process (Poisson-Dirichlet-like) description of the shares.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Supercritical weak convergence to the density-rho* equilibrium is the same statement as local loss of the excess mass to the slow sites.
method: Separate the two regimes. Subcritical rho: the standard route is the coupling/attractiveness argument of Andjel-Ferrari-type plus the classification of extremal invariant measures. Supercritical rho: the claim is that the excess mass escapes locally, so the local law converges to the critical equilibrium.
obstruction: The gap between local equilibrium in the hydrodynamic scaling and t-to-infinity convergence with no rescaling is genuine: the former is a statement about the law at time Nt near site Nx, the latter about the law at site 0 at time t. Bridging them needs a translation-invariance-in-the-environment argument (the environment is not translation invariant for a fixed alpha, only statistically), and that is the concrete wall for the quenched statement.
result: The supercritical half has a clean heuristic that also explains why it should be the harder half: at rho > rho* the excess is not locally visible in the limit because it is stored on the slow sites, whose density tends to zero; so weak convergence to nu at density rho* is a LOCAL LOSS OF MASS statement, and this is exactly the phrase in the abstract of the Bahadoran-Mountford-Ravishankar-Saada PTRF paper found in the status search. The subcritical half reduces, as in the standard ZRP, to showing that the only translation-covariant invariant measures with the given quenched environment are the nu^alpha_phi, which is available in the disordered setting from the same authors' earlier work. So the honest state of this problem is: essentially answered at the level of local equilibrium in the hydrodynamic scaling, with the precise statement asked here (fixed environment, spatially ergodic initial law, t to infinity with no scaling) not confirmed by me.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Particle-hole symmetry gives f_K(rho) = f_K(K-rho); a flat segment exists iff f_K is not strictly concave at its maximum, and the blocking bound gives f_K <= essinf of the rates.
method: Use the particle-hole symmetry of the K-exclusion with site disorder and the variational (Seppalainen) representation of the flux to see what a flat segment would require.
obstruction: Making this rigorous needs the variational formula for f_K in the disordered case, i.e. an analogue of Seppalainen's variational characterisation of the flux, valid for K >= 2 and for site disorder; the known variational formulas are for the homogeneous case or for K = 1 with particle-wise disorder (where the answer is governed by the slowest particle and is known). For site disorder with K >= 2 there is no comparable formula, and the blocking argument only gives the upper bound f_K <= c, not the identification of the interval on which it is attained. That is the wall.
result: Two structural remarks. (1) For site-disordered K-exclusion the flux satisfies f_K(rho) = f_K(K - rho) by particle-hole symmetry, so any flat segment is automatically symmetric about rho = K/2 -- which is why the source states the question at K/2 -- and a flat segment exists if and only if f_K fails to be strictly concave at its maximum. (2) The mechanism producing the flat segment in the disordered ZRP is the saturation of the fugacity at the infimum of the rates; the exclusion analogue is a blocking site whose service rate is close to the infimum, and the current cannot exceed the throughput of the slowest site in the system. In an infinite system with i.i.d. rates bounded below by c > 0 with c in the support, there are arbitrarily long stretches of arbitrarily slow sites, so the maximal current over the whole line is c, and the flat segment is exactly the set of densities at which the system is limited by these slow stretches rather than by the density. This gives a testable prediction: the flat segment is nonempty if and only if the disorder distribution puts mass near its infimum fast enough that a slow stretch of length L occurs within distance exp(o(L)); for i.i.d. rates that is automatic, so a flat segment is predicted for EVERY nondegenerate i.i.d. site disorder.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Spectral gap gives exponential convergence for dnu/dpi in L^2; the conjecture is exactly the singular-nu case, i.e. an L^1-to-L^2 regularisation that fails uniformly because no log-Sobolev inequality holds for a degenerate Dirichlet form.
method: Locate the exact failure of the standard route. Convergence to equilibrium from an arbitrary initial law with an infection is usually obtained from (a) attractiveness plus a coupling, or (b) a spectral gap plus a relative-entropy or hypercontractivity argument started from an absolutely continuous law. The source records that FA-1f is not attractive, which kills (a).
obstruction: The concrete wall is that the only known mechanism transporting an infection across a long healthy stretch is the front/contact-process comparison of the high-q results, whose comparison constant degenerates as q decreases to 0 because the bootstrap-percolation length scale exp(c/q) exceeds the reach of the comparison. Below that threshold there is no known way to show an isolated infection survives, and indeed survival of a single infection for all q is itself unproved.
result: Route (b) fails for a reason that can be stated sharply and that I believe is the real content of the difficulty. The stationary process has a positive spectral gap for every q > 0 in d = 1 (this is classical for FA-1f), so E_nu(f(eta(t))) tends to pi(f) exponentially fast for every nu with density dnu/dpi in L^2(pi). The conjecture concerns nu SINGULAR with respect to pi -- for example the Dirac mass on a single infection at the origin -- for which the L^2 norm is infinite and the gap gives nothing. The natural repair is a hypercontractivity or ultracontractivity estimate turning L^1 or L^infinity data into L^2 data after a short time, but the KCM semigroup is not hypercontractive: the constraint c_x vanishes on a set of positive measure, so the Dirichlet form is degenerate and no logarithmic Sobolev inequality with a finite constant holds uniformly in the volume. So the honest reduction is: Conjecture 1 is equivalent to an L^1-to-L^2 regularisation statement for the FA-1f semigroup at all q, which is false in the uniform-in-time form and must be replaced by a statement quantified by the initial density of infections.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Exponential relaxation follows from any subexponential bound T(l,q) <= exp(o(l)) on the finite-volume relaxation time of a box of size l containing at least one infection.
method: Try to reduce to a finite-volume statement. Under the hypothesis the initial law has an infection within distance l of the origin except with probability exp(-kappa l); on that event one wants to relax the box [-l,l] in time exp(o(l)).
obstruction: The wall is the same as in D0026 but quantitative: no bound on T(l,q) is known that is uniform over initial configurations with a single infection, because the worst case is an infection at the edge of a completely healthy box, and moving it across requires the front to advance, whose speed is only controlled by contact-process comparison at large q. A second obstacle is that the hypothesis is on nu but the dynamics can locally heal all infections in a region, so the property 'an infection within distance l' is not preserved in time; a proof needs a renewal or restart argument that the source explicitly says is unavailable because of non-attractiveness.
result: The reduction is clean and isolates a single missing ingredient: a bound on the FINITE-VOLUME relaxation time of FA-1f in a box of size l with at least one infection present, valid for all q. If T(l,q) denotes that relaxation time, then the hypothesis plus a union bound gives exponential convergence at rate min(kappa/2, 1/T(l,q)) with l chosen of order t, so exponential relaxation holds as soon as T(l,q) grows subexponentially in l for fixed q. In equilibrium T is O(1) by the spectral gap, but the conditioning on a single infection destroys the product structure and the known bounds on the constrained relaxation time carry the bootstrap-percolation length exp(c/q), which is l-independent -- so in fact the reduction shows the conjecture would follow from any bound T(l,q) <= exp(o(l)) uniform over configurations with one infection in the box.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: The representation needs pi conditioned on {BP(eta)=beta} to be a product/Markov measure off the frozen region; this holds for East by (2.6) but fails for two-sided constraints in d >= 2.
method: Look at what the two proved cases have in common. The East proof uses that the bootstrap-percolation closure of a single vacancy is the whole forward cone P_x^+, so the stable configurations are parametrised by antichains I, and pi_beta is a product measure. The d = 1 and translation-invariant proofs go through an entropy-production (Holley-Stroock, Liggett Chapter IV.5) argument.
obstruction: In d >= 2 the event {BP(eta) = beta} depends on the whole configuration through a percolation-type non-local condition, so pi_beta has long-range dependence along the boundary of the frozen region, and the entropy-production argument only sees local Dirichlet forms. In d = 2 the source itself notes the argument of Liggett IV.5 fails, and I could not repair it: the sum of the local entropy productions telescopes only when the constraint is one-sided (East) or the volume is one-dimensional.
result: The obstruction can be pinned to one property. The entropy-production argument controls the Dirichlet form of mu relative to pi and concludes that mu is supported on configurations where every unconstrained site is at equilibrium; to conclude the mixture representation one needs that CONDITIONING ON THE BOOTSTRAP CLOSURE makes the remaining sites independent, i.e. that pi_beta is a product measure on the complement of the frozen region. That is true for East (equation (2.6) of the source) because the closure of a vacancy set is a union of forward cones and the constraint is one-sided. For a two-sided constraint such as FA-1f in d >= 2, the event {BP(eta) = beta} is not a cylinder-decomposable event: it constrains the configuration on the boundary of the frozen region in a non-product way (the boundary must fail to grow), so pi_beta is a boundary-conditioned measure, not a product. Hence the conjecture as stated is a statement about the Gibbs-like structure of pi conditioned on a bootstrap-percolation event, and the missing ingredient is exactly a Markov/DLR property for that conditioning.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Hilbert: R^H equivalent to alpha; l_1, l_inf, c_0: R^B = 2 beta; conjectured dichotomy by B-convexity (uniform containment of l_1^n).
method: Read the two known endpoints as a local-Banach-space statement. Hilbert space gives alpha; l_1, l_inf and c_0 give exactly 2 beta. These are the extreme cases of type and cotype, so conjecture that the dichotomy is governed by B-convexity (equivalently, by whether B contains l_1^n uniformly, by the Giesy-James theorem).
obstruction: Transferring Maurey-Pisier is the wall: the covariance bilinear form is evaluated on SIMPLE random variables with the sup-norm normalisation, so what is needed is a finite-dimensional statement about the norm of the covariance form on B_n x B_n* for finite-dimensional subspaces B_n, with constants depending only on the type/cotype constants. I have no such estimate, and the known interpolation-theoretic comparisons in the references of the source are for the specific coefficients alpha, beta, rho, phi rather than for a general B.
result: The conjecture I can state precisely is: R^B is equivalent to beta if B contains l_1^n uniformly (B not B-convex), and equivalent to alpha otherwise. The 'if' half has a mechanism: the construction of [47, Theorem 3.1] giving R^B = 2 beta for l_1 uses only that the unit ball of B contains an almost-isometric copy of the l_1^n ball on which the covariance form can be made to compute the total variation distance between the joint law and the product law, which is exactly beta; a uniform l_1^n embedding is enough to run it up to an arbitrarily small loss, which is all that 'equivalence' requires. The 'only if' half would follow from a Maurey-Pisier type statement transferred to the bilinear covariance form. Note also that the question presupposes a dichotomy: since beta is strictly stronger than alpha, a third equivalence class strictly between them is not excluded a priori, and I could not exclude it.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: rho(A,C) <= 2 phi(A,C)^{1/2} for any two sigma-fields, so phi* -> 0 implies rho* -> 0; the question is whether phi -> 0 implies phi* -> 0.
method: Compare the two-sided (past/future) and interlaced settings. The classical Cogburn-Ibragimov inequality rho(A,C) <= 2 phi(A,C)^{1/2} holds for ANY two sigma-fields, so the whole question is whether phi-mixing of the past/future pairs forces smallness of phi (or of rho) for INTERLACED pairs, i.e. whether phi(n) -> 0 implies phi*(n) -> 0.
obstruction: The concrete wall is the missing exactness/prescription theorem for phi. The Kesten-O'Brien style constructions realise prescribed rates for alpha, rho, rho*; to build a counterexample one needs a construction that simultaneously forces phi(n) -> 0 (a strong, conditional-probability-uniform requirement) and keeps a fixed interlaced correlation, and the conditional-probability uniformity of phi is precisely what the cutting-and-stacking constructions do not control.
result: The reduction is exact: since rho <= 2 phi^{1/2} for arbitrary pairs of sigma-fields, phi*(n) -> 0 implies rho*(n) -> 0, so a positive answer to Question 2 would follow from 'phi-mixing implies phi*-mixing'. Conversely a counterexample must have phi(n) -> 0 with rho*(n) bounded away from 0, and by the survey's Theorem 4.5 the coefficients rho and rho* can be prescribed essentially arbitrarily and independently for stationary sequences, which is exactly the kind of freedom a counterexample needs; that freedom is why I regard Philipp's negative expectation as the better bet. What blocks the direct construction is that Theorem 4.5 prescribes alpha, rho and rho* but says nothing about phi, and the survey records that no comparable exactness result is known for phi (this is the content of Question 7, recorded here as D0035).

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: rho(n) -> 0 forbids a normalised past/future pair with correlation bounded below; bilateral determinism only produces a straddling pair.
method: Separate what rho-mixing does and does not force. rho(n) -> 0 forces triviality of the ordinary tail sigma-field (a rho-mixing sequence is mixing in the ergodic-theoretic sense, hence has trivial tail by Kolmogorov-type arguments), but bilateral determinism is a statement about the DOUBLE tail, which can be everything even for very strongly mixing sequences.
obstruction: The wall is quantitative: rho-mixing forbids any single normalised pair of past/future functions with correlation bounded below, but the reconstruction map is a function of the WHOLE double tail, and there is no known way to extract from it a single past/future pair with a non-vanishing normalised correlation. An impossibility proof would need such an extraction; a construction would need a cutting-and-stacking scheme with quantitative rho decay, and the existing schemes (which give strong mixing) have rho(n) = 1 for all n because the marker structure creates a bounded pair of indicator functions with correlation bounded below.
result: The known bilaterally deterministic examples with strong mixing are built by cutting-and-stacking with an intricate coding that reconstructs the middle of a word from the two far ends. The obstruction to making them rho-mixing can be localised: rho-mixing means the correlation of ANY two square-integrable functions of past and future decays, and for a finite-state sequence the space of such functions is spanned by cylinder indicators, so rho(n) -> 0 forces sup over cylinder pairs of the normalised covariance to vanish. Bilateral determinism, on the other hand, produces a sequence of pairs (f_m, g_m) -- the two far ends of a word -- whose joint function determines the middle symbol exactly; the correlation of X_0 with the pair (f_m, g_m) is therefore bounded below uniformly in m. That does NOT immediately contradict rho(n) -> 0, because the pair straddles the origin rather than sitting in a past/future pair separated by n. So the two properties are compatible at the level of this argument, and the question is genuinely about whether the reconstruction can be arranged with a correlation that is spread thinly over many cylinders.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Ornstein: isomorphic to a Bernoulli shift iff very weak Bernoulli; the missing step is a rate-free dbar estimate.
method: Use Ornstein's criterion: X is isomorphic to a Bernoulli shift iff it is very weak Bernoulli (VWB). So the question is whether alpha(n) -> 0 implies VWB for finite-state processes.
obstruction: The concrete wall: dbar-distance is not controlled by any single mixing coefficient without a rate, because dbar is a per-coordinate average of a coupling cost over a window of length n, and n mixing coefficients each of size alpha(m) can sum to something of order n alpha(m) which is useless unless alpha decays. Converting decorrelation into coupling without a rate would need a compactness/limiting argument in the space of processes, and the class of strongly mixing finite-state processes is not compact in dbar.
result: The gap can be stated as a rate gap and that is the honest summary. VWB requires the conditional law of (X_1,...,X_n) given the past to be within dbar-distance eps of the unconditional law, for n large, and the standard route bounds dbar by a sum of the mixing coefficients over a window of length n, which needs sum-type control, i.e. a rate. The Penn State result found in the status search (finite-state phi-mixing processes that are not VWB with rate O(1/n)) shows the rate cannot be improved for free even under phi-mixing, so the residual question is genuinely about qualitative alpha(n) -> 0 with no rate. My reading: an affirmative answer would have to produce a dbar estimate that is not a sum of mixing coefficients, i.e. an argument using the finiteness of the state space to convert a qualitative decorrelation into a coupling; no such mechanism is known.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: One gap: rho <= 2 phi(n)^{1/2} by Cogburn-Ibragimov plus the Markov property; the supremum over arbitrarily many alternations is what is uncontrolled.
method: Exploit the Markov property. For a Markov chain, phi-mixing is equivalent to a Doeblin-type condition (by Theorem 3.3(2) of the source, phi(n) < 1/2 for some n forces exponential decay), so under the hypothesis the chain is uniformly ergodic. Then try to reduce the interlaced coefficient rho*(n) to a product over the gaps between the blocks of the two interlaced index sets.
obstruction: The wall is the unbounded number of blocks: rho*(n) takes a supremum over ALL pairs of interlaced index sets, hence over arbitrarily many alternations, and each alternation can contribute a fresh correlation of size comparable to rho(n) even if each individual gap is strongly decoupling. This is exactly the mechanism behind the known example (reference [36] of the source) of a stationary countable-state Markov chain that is rho-mixing but not rho*-mixing, so the Markov property alone cannot close the gap; what is needed is that phi-mixing, unlike rho-mixing, controls conditional probabilities uniformly and therefore might survive the alternations. Making that precise requires a multi-gap version of the Cogburn-Ibragimov inequality, which I do not have.
result: The reduction works block by block and identifies exactly where it fails. Let S and T be interlaced index sets with all gaps at least n. Order the blocks along Z; by the Markov property, conditionally on the variables in any one gap, the configuration to the left is independent of the configuration to the right. Uniform ergodicity gives, for each gap, a total-variation contraction by a factor at most phi(n). If there were only ONE gap, rho over that gap would be at most 2 phi(n)^{1/2}, giving the result. With k gaps, the naive bound multiplies k contraction factors but the functions involved are not products, so one only gets a bound of the form min(1, k * something) rather than a product, and the supremum defining rho* is over all k.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Instantaneous functions of Harris recurrent chains are exactly the processes with an i.i.d. regeneration-block decomposition.
method: Compare the two representation classes. An instantaneous function of a stationary Harris recurrent chain has a regeneration structure: the chain hits a small set infinitely often and the excursions between successive regeneration times are i.i.d. So such a process is a 'renewal-block' process. The question is therefore whether every psi-mixing (or 1-dependent) stationary process admits such a regeneration.
obstruction: The wall is that the Harris class is very large: the underlying chain may take values in an arbitrary space, so any process with an exponentially mixing regeneration is included, and it is hard to name a property of a psi-mixing process that forbids regeneration. A candidate invariant would be an entropy or a coding-length obstruction, but psi-mixing already forces exponential decay of all the coefficients and gives no room for such an obstruction.
result: The right invariant to look at is the regeneration structure, and it gives a concrete route to a negative answer. If X is an instantaneous function of a Harris recurrent chain, then X is a block factor of an i.i.d. sequence in the weak sense that it decomposes into i.i.d. blocks of random length with a geometric-type tail (under uniform ergodicity, exponential). 1-dependent processes are known NOT all to be 1-block factors of i.i.d. sequences: the Aaronson-Gilat-Keane-de Valk example is a 1-dependent 3-state process that is not a 1-block factor. That example is the natural candidate here, and the honest statement is that the question reduces to whether it (or a variant) admits any regeneration at all. My attempt at the reduction found no obstruction to regeneration for that particular example, so a genuinely new construction is likely needed.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Bradley [43, Thm 22.14] as quoted in the source: for strictly stationary X, phi(n) < 1/2 for some n implies phi(n) -> 0. Hence b_n = 1/4 for all n is unrealisable.
method: Check the literal statement against the constraints on phi already recorded in the same survey before attempting any construction.
obstruction: Characterising the realisable phi-sequences is where I stop. The constraints above are necessary; I have no further necessary conditions and no matching construction. The known constructions (Kesten-O'Brien and its descendants) prescribe alpha, rho and rho* exactly (Theorem 4.5 of the source) but only prescribe phi up to an arbitrarily small window, because phi is a supremum of conditional probabilities and the cutting-and-stacking constructions control measures of sets, not conditional probabilities uniformly over the past. That uniformity is the wall.
result: The literal general form of Question 7 is FALSE, and the counterexample is one line from the survey's own text. On PDF p. 18 the source quotes, from [43, Theorem 22.14], the following for a strictly stationary sequence with NO ergodicity assumption: 'If phi(n) < 1/2 for some n >= 1, then X is phi-mixing', i.e. phi(n) -> 0. Take b_n = 1/4 for every n: it is nonincreasing and lies in [0,1], but any stationary X with phi(1) = 1/4 has phi(n) -> 0, so phi(n) = 1/4 for all n is impossible. More generally no nonincreasing sequence that drops below 1/2 without converging to 0 is realisable, and Theorem 4.1(3)(c) adds that for an ergodic-theoretically mixing sequence either phi(n) -> 0 or phi(n) = 1 for all n. So the realisable set of phi-sequences is strictly smaller than all nonincreasing [0,1]-sequences, and the substantive residual problem is to CHARACTERISE it. The source's own sub-question (is 1 > phi(1) = phi(2) > 0 = phi(3) realisable?) is not touched by these constraints, since phi(3) = 0 makes X 2-dependent and phi(1) may exceed 1/2.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Theorem 6.5 characterises 'r*(1) < 1 and r*(n) -> 0' as continuous positive spectral density; the residual class is the r*(1) = 1 degeneracy.
method: Isolate what dropping the hypothesis r*(1) < 1 costs. Theorem 6.5 shows continuity and positivity of the spectral density f is equivalent to r*(1) < 1 together with r*(n) -> 0; so the question is which spectral densities give r*(n) -> 0 with r*(1) = 1.
obstruction: The wall is that r* is a supremum over interlaced index sets of arbitrarily many blocks, so it is not the norm of a single Toeplitz or Hankel operator but a supremum of norms of compressions to arbitrarily complicated subspaces. All the classical spectral characterisations (Helson-Sarason for rho, Kolmogorov-Rozanov for the linear coefficients) reduce to a single Hankel operator, and that reduction is unavailable here.
result: The residual class can be described structurally, which is the content of this attempt. r*(1) = 1 means some finite interlaced pair of index sets at distance 1 already has maximal correlation 1, which for a CCWS sequence means the closed linear spans of two such families of variables touch at angle zero; this is a degeneracy of the sequence at lag 1 and is not a property of the smoothness of f but of its vanishing or of its unboundedness. Since r*(n) -> 0 is a statement about all interlaced pairs at distance n, and the operator whose norm computes r* is (a compression of) the Toeplitz operator with symbol f, the natural conjecture is: r*(n) -> 0 holds iff f is the sum of a continuous positive function and a function whose Toeplitz operator is compact on the relevant subspaces, i.e. iff f has continuous positive part with the singular set concentrated on a set that becomes invisible to interlaced blocks at large separation. Concretely I expect the answer to be: r*(n) -> 0 iff f = g h with g continuous and positive and log h in a Sarason-type space (VMO-like), which is the standard shape of the answers for r(n) and zeta(n).

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: For Gaussian sequences rho*(n) = r*(n), so Questions 8 and 9 coincide on the Gaussian class.
method: Use the Gaussian reduction. For a stationary Gaussian sequence, rho for any pair of sigma-fields generated by families of the variables equals the maximal correlation of the corresponding Gaussian subspaces, so rho*(n) equals the supremum over interlaced index sets at distance n of the cosine of the angle between the two closed linear spans. So the problem is purely a question about the geometry of the Toeplitz operator with symbol f.
obstruction: Same wall as D0036: rho* is a supremum over arbitrarily many interlaced blocks and is not the norm of a single Hankel operator, so the Helson-Sarason machinery (which characterises the norm of one Hankel operator with symbol the conjugate function) does not apply. The known sufficient direction (continuous positive f implies rho*(n) -> 0) is Theorem 6.5; the converse requires ruling out spectral densities with a zero or a pole that is invisible to every finite interlaced configuration, and I have no argument for that.
result: The Gaussian case therefore reduces to exactly the same operator-theoretic problem as Question 8 (D0036), which is a structural observation worth recording: for Gaussian sequences, rho*(n) = r*(n), so Questions 8 and 9 of the source are literally the same problem restricted to Gaussian sequences, and any solution of one gives the other in that class. The classical rho-answer is Helson-Sarason: rho(n) -> 0 iff f = |P|^2 exp(u + v-tilde) with u, v real continuous and P a polynomial with no zeros in the open disc; the natural rho* conjecture drops the polynomial factor and demands f = exp(u + v-tilde) with u continuous and v continuous (no zeros allowed at all), which matches Theorem 6.5 of the source in the direction where both are known.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Tail-measurability forces zero entropy rate; a nondegenerate finite-state field with a 1-dependence across half-space boundaries should have positive entropy rate.
method: Ask what the real-valued construction uses that a finite alphabet does not have. Half-space 1-dependence plus tail-measurability means the field reconstructs itself from arbitrarily distant information while being nearly independent across half-space boundaries -- a reconstruction that in the real-valued construction can hide unboundedly much information in a single real coordinate.
obstruction: The tension above is heuristic at exactly one point: 'lattice half-space 1-dependence' as used in the source's reference [28] is a condition on two half-spaces separated by a lattice distance one, not an independence of a single site from a half-space, so it does not directly lower-bound the entropy rate of the field by the single-site entropy. Constructing the correct entropy inequality requires the technical definitions of that paper, which are not reproduced in the survey and which I did not fetch. So the honest state is: an entropy obstruction is the natural route to a negative answer, and it needs the exact definition of half-space 1-dependence to be turned into a proof.
result: The obstruction is an entropy budget, and stating it is the useful output here. In the real-valued construction each site can carry an infinite amount of information, so the tail can determine the field by encoding it in the digits of the coordinates. With a finite alphabet the entropy per site is at most log |alphabet|, and tail-measurability forces the process to have zero entropy: if the field is measurable with respect to its tail then the entropy rate must vanish, because conditional entropy given the tail is the entropy rate and it is zero. But half-space 1-dependence forces a positive entropy rate unless the field is degenerate: 1-dependence across a half-space boundary means the conditional law of a site given the far half-space is close to its unconditional law, so the entropy rate is at least the entropy of one site minus a term controlled by the dependence, which is positive for a nondegenerate finite-state field. This looks like a genuine tension and would settle the question in the NEGATIVE for finite alphabets -- but the argument as stated is not complete, see the obstruction.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Nesting holds iff the tridiagonal entries are independent and truncation reproduces the lower-size model; true for Hermite, Laguerre, Jacobi and CMV, false for general V.
method: Identify what makes the beta-Hermite nesting work. In the Dumitriu-Edelman tridiagonal model the entries are independent chi and Gaussian variables, so the top-left minor of size m is literally the beta-Hermite model of size m with the same beta; the nesting is a consequence of the INDEPENDENCE of the tridiagonal entries.
obstruction: The wall is that nesting is an exact distributional identity, and outside the classical families the tridiagonal entries have a nearest-neighbour dependence that survives truncation as a boundary term. One could ask for an asymptotic nesting (agreement up to a vanishing total-variation error), which is likely true by universality, but the question as posed asks for an exact coupling and I have no candidate beyond the classical three.
result: The mechanism localises the answer: a tridiagonal (Jacobi-matrix) model has the nesting property exactly when its entries are independent and the law of the top-left m x m block is the law of the size-m model. For the classical beta-ensembles this is true for Hermite and Laguerre (Dumitriu-Edelman) and for the circular ensemble in its CMV (Killip-Nenciu) form, where the Verblunsky coefficients are independent and the truncation is again a CbetaE of lower size; so the answer is affirmative for the three classical families and for Jacobi. For a general potential V the tridiagonalisation produces entries whose joint density does NOT factor (the source itself notes that for quartic V it factors only into functions of two consecutive pairs), so the minors are not the same model at lower size and the nesting fails at the level of exact laws.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Hard-edge distribution = hitting probability of the Riccati diffusion for the stochastic Bessel operator; equation (10) is its backward equation.
method: Ask what kind of object the check has to be. Equation (10) is an identity satisfied by the hard-edge limiting distribution expressed through the stochastic Bessel operator; Mo's formulas are explicit integrable-systems expressions. A check is a proof that an explicit special function solves a PDE/ODE coming from a diffusion generator.
obstruction: The computational task is where it stops: Mo's formulas are given as Fredholm-determinant or Painleve-type expressions in variables that are not the diffusion's natural coordinates, and the change of variables that would make the backward operator recognisable is not available in closed form. The same obstacle is what makes the bulk analogue (Question 9, recorded here as D0047) open.
result: The natural route is to convert the operator-side identity into a Feynman-Kac representation and then verify that Mo's formula is the corresponding transition density. Concretely: the stochastic Bessel operator's smallest eigenvalue has a Riccati/diffusion representation (Ramirez-Rider), so the hard-edge distribution function is a hitting probability for an explicit one-dimensional diffusion; equation (10) is the Kolmogorov backward equation for that hitting probability. So the check reduces to verifying that Mo's expression, viewed as a function of the boundary parameter, satisfies that backward equation with the right boundary behaviour -- a purely computational task, not a conceptual one.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Sine_beta counting function = winding of a hyperbolic diffusion; k-point correlations = joint winding of k diffusions driven by one Brownian motion.
method: Look for the operator-side object that the correlation formulas would come from. For a random Schrodinger operator, k-point correlations of eigenvalues are expectations of products of spectral shift/counting functions, so what is needed is a formula for the joint law of the eigenvalue counting function at several energies.
obstruction: The k coupled windings are driven by one Brownian motion and are therefore strongly dependent, with the dependence encoded in a matrix Riccati equation whose stationary law is not known for k >= 2; the k=1 stationary law (which yields the gap asymptotics) is available only because the one-dimensional Riccati equation has an explicit invariant density. That missing stationary law is the wall.
result: For the bulk this is available in principle and that is the useful observation: the Brownian carousel gives the counting function N(lambda) of Sine_beta as the winding number of an explicit hyperbolic diffusion, so the joint law of (N(lambda_1),...,N(lambda_k)) is the joint law of k coupled windings driven by the SAME Brownian motion. Multi-point correlation asymptotics therefore reduce to a large-deviation or Gaussian-fluctuation analysis for a k-dimensional degenerate diffusion, and the known one-point results (the Valko-Virag gap probability asymptotics) are exactly the k=1 case of this programme. So Question 4 is, in the bulk, a concrete question about a k-dimensional hyperbolic diffusion.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Scaling t -> ct: kinetic c^{-2}, potential c^{1/(2k+1)}, noise c^{-k/(2k+1)-1/2}; the three balance simultaneously, so the ansatz is critical.
method: Check the conjecture for internal consistency by scaling, which is the cheapest way to test an operator ansatz. Under t -> c t the three terms scale as c^{-2}, c^{1/(2k+1)} and c^{-k/(2k+1)-1/2} (white noise picks up an extra c^{-1/2}).
obstruction: The proof route (as for the k = 0 case) is a tridiagonal-to-operator convergence argument requiring (i) a tightness estimate for the quadratic form and (ii) control of the singular multiplication operator t^{-k/(2k+1)} b'. Item (ii) is the wall: for k >= 1 the noise coefficient BLOWS UP at t = 0 like a negative power, so the operator is not obviously self-adjoint or bounded below without a Hardy-type inequality, and the standard form-boundedness argument used for the stochastic Airy operator (where the noise coefficient is constant) does not apply. Establishing the essential self-adjointness of S_{beta,k} is a prerequisite that is not addressed in the source.
result: The ansatz is scaling-consistent in exactly the right way, which is a nontrivial check the source does not carry out. Balancing the kinetic term against the potential requires c^{-2} = c^{1/(2k+1)}, i.e. the natural scale exponent is fixed; the noise term then scales as c^{-k/(2k+1)-1/2}, and substituting the balance exponent shows the noise scales at the SAME rate as the other two terms, so the operator is critical, which is the necessary condition for it to be a scaling limit. For k = 0 the formula degenerates to the stochastic Airy operator -d^2 + t + (2/sqrt beta) b', which is the proved case, so the family interpolates correctly. I also checked the exponent against the beta = 2 higher-order Tracy-Widom literature found in the status search: the higher-order kernels there have edge exponent matching a density vanishing like x^{2k+1/2}, consistent with the conjectured operator.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Every k-th eigenvalue = Prufer phase divided by k = a k-fold time change of the Brownian carousel.
method: Ask what decimation does to the spectral data. At the finite level decimation is a statement about superposition/decimation of eigenvalue point processes; at the operator level the eigenvalues are the spectrum of a random Schrodinger or Dirac operator, so a coupling would be an operator-valued construction whose spectrum is every k-th eigenvalue of another operator.
obstruction: Checking it requires matching the drift and diffusion coefficients of the two carousel SDEs after the time change, and the carousel SDE's parameters depend on beta both through the noise strength and through the deterministic angular drift; the time change fixes one and breaks the other, so a compensating change of the hyperbolic metric is needed and I could not find one. At the edge there is no carousel and the corresponding statement would have to be made for the Riccati flow of the stochastic Airy operator, where the decimation has no evident meaning.
result: There is a natural candidate and it is worth recording. Taking every k-th eigenvalue of a one-dimensional Schrodinger operator is, via the oscillation theorem, the statement that the Prufer phase advances by k pi rather than pi; so the decimated operator should be the operator whose Prufer phase is the original phase divided by k. In the bulk this is implementable: the Sine_beta operator's counting function is the winding of the hyperbolic carousel, and dividing the winding by k is a time change of the carousel. So the conjectural coupling is: the beta = 2k carousel is the beta = 2/k carousel run at a k-fold slower angular speed. This is a concrete, checkable statement, which is the output of this attempt.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Random Jacobi coefficients = deterministic ones + n^{-1/2} Gaussian field; the limiting operator is the deterministic Sturm-Liouville operator plus white noise.
method: Compare the two three-term recurrences. The deterministic orthogonal polynomials for weight e^{-V} satisfy a recurrence with deterministic Jacobi coefficients (a_i, b_i); the beta-ensemble tridiagonal model has random (a_i, b_i) whose means are, to leading order, the deterministic ones.
obstruction: Making this a theorem for general beta requires controlling the polynomials themselves, not just the coefficients: a small perturbation of the recurrence coefficients can produce a large change in the polynomials in the oscillatory region, and the transfer-matrix products are only controlled after a Prufer-phase change of variables that is available at the edge (giving the stochastic Airy operator) but not uniformly across the bulk. Uniform control across the bulk is the wall.
result: The correct statement of the relation is a concentration statement plus a fluctuation statement, and separating them is the useful step. Leading order: the random Jacobi coefficients concentrate on the deterministic ones, with the equilibrium measure of V as the common limiting spectral measure; this is standard. Fluctuation order: the difference between the random and deterministic recurrence coefficients is, after centring and scaling by sqrt(n), an explicit Gaussian field, and it is this field that produces the noise term in the limiting operators. So the answer to the first half of the question is: the random polynomials are the deterministic ones perturbed by an n^{-1/2} Gaussian field in the recurrence coefficients, and the limiting operator is the deterministic Sturm-Liouville operator (whose spectrum is the equilibrium measure) plus white noise.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Ansatz H_t = -d^2 + x + (2/sqrt beta) W(x,t), W white in x and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck in t; the marginals must be the stochastic Airy operator.
method: Ask what object the limit should be. Hermitian Brownian motion has eigenvalues evolving as Dyson Brownian motion; at the edge and in the bulk the local limits of DBM are known point-process-valued dynamics (the Airy and Sine processes in time). An operator limit would be an operator-valued process whose spectrum is that dynamics.
obstruction: The obstruction is that the eigenvalues of an operator-valued OU process do NOT in general perform Dyson Brownian motion: the Ito correction for the eigenvalue of a perturbed operator involves the whole resolvent, and matching it to the DBM repulsion term requires the noise to be a matrix-valued OU with a specific covariance whose continuum limit is not obviously a well-defined noise field. Establishing existence of the operator-valued process with the right eigenvalue dynamics is the wall.
result: The natural candidate is a stochastic-Airy operator with a time-dependent noise, and the consistency requirement pins its correlation structure: the limiting operator process should be H_t = -d^2/dt^2 + x + (2/sqrt beta) W(x, t) where W is a noise that is white in the space variable x and has an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-type correlation in the time variable, with the time scale chosen so that the eigenvalue process has the known local relaxation time (of order n^{-1/3} at the edge, matching the Airy_2 time scale). This ansatz is forced: the marginals must be the stochastic Airy operator, and the eigenvalue dynamics must be Markov, which for a Schrodinger operator with additive noise means the noise itself must be Markov in time, i.e. OU.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Bulk gap probability = survival probability of the carousel winding = solution of a linear backward PDE; Painleve V is a nonlinear reduction that must come from a hidden Riccati structure.
method: Set up the reduction. The bulk gap probability P(no eigenvalue in (-lambda, lambda)) is the probability that the carousel winding stays below 2 pi over the relevant time, i.e. a survival probability for a one-dimensional hyperbolic diffusion with a time-dependent drift, hence a solution of a linear parabolic PDE (the Kolmogorov backward equation for the carousel generator).
obstruction: The wall is that the linear PDE has no obvious separation of variables in the carousel coordinates, and the quantity that closes for beta = 2 (the resolvent kernel of the sine kernel on the interval) has no known carousel-side meaning. Rumanov's hard-edge success used the fact that the Bessel operator's Riccati flow is explicitly integrable, and the carousel's is not.
result: The reduction is exact and identifies the exact form of the missing step: the gap probability is a solution of a LINEAR backward equation in two variables (the hyperbolic coordinate and the time/energy parameter), while Painleve V is a NONLINEAR ODE in the energy alone. Passing from one to the other is a reduction of order that has to come from a special structure -- in the integrable-systems derivation it comes from the Fredholm determinant and its logarithmic derivative satisfying a Riccati chain. So the concrete target is: find the change of variables under which the logarithmic derivative in lambda of the carousel survival probability satisfies a closed equation. For beta = 2 the answer must reproduce Painleve V, so this is a checkable one-parameter problem.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Loop equations = Cameron-Martin/Malliavin integration by parts for the driving white noise of the limiting operator; the Malliavin derivative of an eigenvalue is formally the square of its eigenfunction.
method: Recall the finite-n derivation: the loop equations come from the invariance of the eigenvalue integral under an infinitesimal change of variables lambda_i -> lambda_i + eps f(lambda_i), i.e. from integration by parts against the Vandermonde-weighted density. Ask what the corresponding invariance is for a random operator.
