obstruction: Carrying it out needs the Malliavin differentiability of eigenvalues of the stochastic Airy operator with respect to the driving white noise, together with an explicit formula for the Malliavin derivative in terms of the eigenfunction; the formal answer is the square of the eigenfunction, but making this rigorous requires the eigenfunctions to be in the right Sobolev class, which is delicate because the noise is a distribution. That regularity is the wall. In addition, the finite-n loop equations are a hierarchy in 1/n, and the operator limit has already taken n to infinity, so what one recovers is only the leading equation unless a finite-size correction to the operator is retained.
result: The operator-side analogue of the change of variables is a conjugation of the operator by a one-parameter family of unitaries generated by a function of the operator, and the loop equation should be the resulting integration-by-parts (Cameron-Martin / Girsanov) identity for the white-noise part. Concretely, for the stochastic Airy operator, shifting the noise b' by a deterministic direction h changes the law by an explicit Girsanov density, and the derivative in h of an eigenvalue functional gives an identity between the first and second moments of resolvent traces -- which is the shape of a one-loop equation. So the honest content of this attempt is that the loop equations should be the Malliavin integration-by-parts identities for the noise, and the choice of Cameron-Martin direction corresponds to the choice of test function f in the finite-n derivation.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: d_gamma = 2Q/xi with Q = 2/gamma + gamma/2; d_{sqrt(8/3)} = 4 is known only through the Brownian map bijections.
method: Ask what kind of object d_gamma is. The known relations are d_gamma = 2 Q / xi with Q = 2/gamma + gamma/2, so a formula for d_gamma is the same as a formula for the LFPP exponent xi in terms of gamma. The exponent xi is defined by a subadditive limit for the LFPP distance, so it is a Lyapunov-type exponent for a multiplicative cascade of Gaussian weights.
obstruction: The wall is that no exactly solvable structure is known for the LQG metric away from gamma = sqrt(8/3). Every exponent that has been computed in LQG (measure exponents, the KPZ relation, ball boundary dimensions) is a consequence of the multiplicative structure of the MEASURE, which is exactly solvable; the metric is a first-passage time and is not a function of the measure. This is the same wall that prevents computing the time constant in ordinary first-passage percolation, and there is no reason to think the LQG case is easier except that its environment is exactly scale invariant.
result: The honest structural statement is that d_gamma is a first-passage percolation time constant for a log-correlated environment, and the only quantity of that type with a known closed form in two dimensions is the sqrt(8/3) case, which is known NOT from the metric side at all but from the Brownian-map bijections. That is a strong warning against expecting a closed form: the value 4 is a combinatorial output of the Schaeffer bijection, and no bijection is available for other gamma. Two soft constraints I can record: (i) d_gamma is strictly increasing in gamma (Ding-Gwynne), continuous, with d_0+ = 2 and d_{2-} = 4 * something at criticality; (ii) the Watabiki prediction is false at small gamma (Ding-Goswami), so any conjectural formula must fail to match Watabiki near gamma = 0, which rules out the whole family of formulas obtained by analytic continuation of the Watabiki ansatz.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Route: model to mated-CRT map up to constants, then mated-CRT map to the LQG metric; the polylogarithmic coupling error blocks the first step.
method: Identify what the sqrt(8/3) proof uses and what is available for other gamma. The Miller-Sheffield programme identifies the Brownian map with sqrt(8/3)-LQG using the QLE growth process and the fact that the Brownian map has an intrinsic metric constructed from the Brownian snake; for other gamma there is no discrete metric-space limit theorem at all.
obstruction: The concrete wall is the polylogarithmic loss in the strong coupling of the encoding walk with Brownian motion (the Komlos-Major-Tusnady/Zaitsev rate), which is not good enough for a scaling limit of distances: a Gromov-Hausdorff statement needs distances correct up to a factor tending to 1, whereas the coupling gives them up to a polylogarithmic factor. Removing the loss would require a strong-coupling theorem with error o(n^{eps}) for every eps, which is false in general for the KMT rate.
result: The available discrete input for general gamma is the mating-of-trees convergence, which gives the map together with a space-filling curve in the peanosphere topology, plus the strong-coupling results with the mated-CRT map that give graph distances up to polylogarithmic errors (this is the content of the companion survey by Gwynne, Holden and Sun, recorded in this ledger as D0078-D0090). So the honest reduction is: Problem 5.2 for a given map model follows from (a) an up-to-constants comparison of graph distance in the model with the mated-CRT map, and (b) a Gromov-Hausdorff convergence of the mated-CRT map to the LQG metric. Item (b) is the more likely to be within reach because the mated-CRT map is defined directly from the continuum, and item (a) is exactly what the polylogarithmic strong-coupling errors fail to give.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Naive independent count gives max(0, 2 - alpha^2/2 - (2 - d_geo)); positive correlation with thin points should push the maximiser to negative alpha.
method: Compare with the solved ball-boundary case and see which step transfers. For the ball boundary the dimension is computed by a first-moment count over alpha-thick points weighted by the probability that a thick point lies on the boundary, and the maximiser comes from optimising a concave exponent in alpha.
obstruction: The joint law of the field along a geodesic is exactly what is not available: a geodesic is a measurable function of the whole field and there is no known description of the conditional law of the field given the geodesic (no analogue of the Markov property along an SLE curve). Every existing computation of geodesic properties uses only up-to-constants estimates, which cannot produce a dimension.
result: The same first-moment scheme sets up cleanly for geodesics and identifies the missing input. The number of Euclidean eps-balls containing an alpha-thick point is eps^{-(2 - alpha^2/2)}; the probability that a given eps-ball is hit by the geodesic is eps^{2 - d_geo} where d_geo is the Euclidean dimension of the geodesic. If these two events were independent the answer would be the naive intersection dimension max(0, 2 - alpha^2/2 - d_geo-complement), with a unique maximiser at alpha = 0. But they are strongly positively correlated for alpha of the sign that makes the metric locally SHORT (negative alpha, thin points), because a geodesic prefers to travel through thin points -- the LQG metric assigns small length to regions where the field is low. So the correct exponent involves the joint law and the maximiser should be at a NEGATIVE alpha, in contrast to the ball boundary where it is at the positive value xi. That sign prediction is the output of this attempt and it is testable.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Linear interpolation between d_0 = 2 and d_{sqrt(8/3)} = 4 predicts d_{sqrt 2} = 3.732 > 3.63299, so d_gamma is not affine; Watabiki's value 3.5616 at gamma = sqrt 2 is inside the rigorous window.
method: Use the bounds quoted in this source as a numerical constraint on candidate closed forms, which the other statement of the problem (D0049) does not do.
obstruction: Same wall as D0049: no exactly solvable structure for the metric away from gamma = sqrt(8/3). The numerical eliminations above constrain but do not determine the function.
result: The interval 3.550408 <= d_{sqrt 2} <= 3.63299 is narrow enough to eliminate simple guesses, and doing that elimination is the concrete contribution here. Watabiki's formula gives d_gamma = 1 + gamma^2/4 + sqrt((1+gamma^2/4)^2 + gamma^2), which at gamma = sqrt 2 evaluates to 1.5 + sqrt(2.25 + 2) = 1.5 + 2.0616 = 3.5616, inside the interval -- so the quoted bounds do NOT by themselves refute Watabiki at gamma = sqrt 2 (the refutation of Ding-Goswami is at SMALL gamma, as the source says). The linear interpolation between d_0 = 2 and d_{sqrt(8/3)} = 4 gives 2 + 2*(sqrt2/sqrt(8/3)) = 2 + 2*0.8660 = 3.732, which is ABOVE the upper bound 3.63299 and is therefore refuted; so d_gamma is strictly concave somewhere on (0, sqrt(8/3)) if it is smooth. That concavity is a genuine, checkable consequence of the quoted bounds that I did not find stated in either source.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Embedded convergence needs a model-specific embedding from a statistical-mechanics observable plus a two-independent-copies joint convergence theorem.
method: Look at the embedded (conformal) half of the statement, which the other formulation (D0050) does not emphasise, and ask what the Cardy-embedding proof for uniform triangulations used.
obstruction: For spanning-tree-weighted maps (gamma = sqrt 2) the natural observable is the Mullin-bijection walk, and the two-copies statement is exactly Problem 6.4 for that model; for Ising-weighted maps (gamma = sqrt 3) the corresponding bijection is the hamburger-cheeseburger encoding whose walk is non-Markovian, so even the strong coupling with Brownian motion is unavailable (Problem 6.2 of the other survey, D0081 here). Those two are the walls.
result: The embedded convergence for uniform triangulations (Holden-Sun) is proved via the Cardy embedding, whose definition uses percolation observables on the map, and the key probabilistic input is the joint convergence of the map with TWO independent percolation configurations (this is Problem 6.4 of the mating-of-trees survey, recorded here as D0083). So the honest statement is that for each new model one needs an embedding defined from an observable of the corresponding statistical mechanics model plus a two-independent-copies joint convergence theorem for that observable. That is a concrete programme, model by model, and it is why the general statement is hard: it is not one theorem but a family indexed by the decorating model.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Tightness is dimension-agnostic; uniqueness in 2D uses the infinite-dimensional conformal group, which by Liouville's theorem does not exist for n >= 3.
method: Check whether the two-dimensional construction's key inputs have n-dimensional analogues. The 2D construction goes through Liouville first passage percolation: mollify the field, define the length of a path as the integral of exp(xi h_eps) along it, prove tightness of the normalised metric, then prove uniqueness of the subsequential limit from a list of axioms.
obstruction: The wall is the rigidity of conformal maps in dimension >= 3 (Liouville's theorem): the uniqueness argument in 2D uses the infinite-dimensional conformal group to transport the metric between subdomains, and in higher dimensions that group is finite dimensional and cannot do the job. A replacement would have to be a purely metric-measure characterisation, e.g. by a Weyl scaling plus a Markov property with respect to arbitrary subdomains, and no such characterisation is known.
result: Two of the three steps transfer verbatim and one does not, and locating the failure is the useful output. (a) The mollified LFPP metric is defined in every dimension with no change. (b) The tightness proof rests on a multiplicative-chaos-style moment bound plus the Efron-Stein/percolation argument for the concentration of distances, both of which are dimension-agnostic. (c) The UNIQUENESS axioms include the Weyl scaling relation and, crucially, a locality/Markov property of the field, and the axiomatic characterisation of Gwynne-Miller uses conformal covariance -- an essentially two-dimensional input, since the Weyl transformation of the metric under a conformal map has no analogue for n >= 3 (conformal maps of R^n for n >= 3 are Mobius by Liouville's theorem, an extremely rigid family). So the existence half of the problem is plausibly within reach in every dimension, and the uniqueness half is genuinely two-dimensional.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: P(X_n = 0) = (1 - m E(X_n) + E(X_{n+1}))^{1/m}; the package reduces to identifying the universal constant 2/(m-1) in E(m^{X_n}) - 1 ~ 2/((m-1) n).
method: Use the source's own Lemma 4 identity P(X_n = 0) = (1 - m E(X_n) + E(X_{n+1}))^{1/m} and the generating-function recursion to see what the conjecture is equivalent to.
obstruction: The proved bounds of Theorem 3 have constants c_1, c_2 depending on m with a gap of order sqrt(Lambda_0 / P(X_0=0)), i.e. depending on the initial law, whereas the conjectured constant 2/(m-1) is universal. Closing the gap requires a renewal or fixed-point argument showing the recursion forgets its initial law at the critical point, and the natural candidate -- a smoothing/contraction estimate for the map on generating functions -- degenerates exactly at criticality because the linearisation has spectral radius 1. That is the wall.
result: The four conjectures form a tight logical package, and disentangling it is the useful step. From Lemma 4, Conjecture 1 (survival probability asymptotic to 4/((m-1)^2 n^2)) plus the source's Lemma 5 implies Conjecture 3 (E(X_n) asymptotic to 4m/((m-1)^3 n^2)), as the source itself notes. Conversely, Conjecture 2 (conditional geometric limit with P(Y_infinity = k) = (m-1)/m^k) plus Conjecture 1 gives Conjecture 3 immediately since the conditional mean of the geometric law is m/(m-1). And Theorem 3 of the source, which is proved, gives E(m^{X_n}) - 1 of exact order 1/n, which is the b) half of Conjecture 4 up to the constant. So the whole package reduces to identifying the CONSTANT in the proved 1/n order of E(m^{X_n}) - 1, namely showing it equals 2/(m-1); Conjecture 4b then gives Conjecture 1 through the generating-function relation. That is a sharp reduction: the qualitative rate is already a theorem, and only the constant is missing.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: The geometric law with ratio 1/m is the fixed point of the m-tilting operation; Conjecture 2 is a Yaglom limit for the recursion conditioned on non-extinction.
method: Ask why the geometric law with ratio 1/m should be the fixed point. The critical condition is (m-1) E(X_0 m^{X_0}) = E(m^{X_0}), which is a statement about the tilted law with density proportional to m^{x}; so the natural object is the m-tilt of the law of X_n.
obstruction: Item (i) is the wall: the conditional law given survival could a priori escape to infinity, since the recursion adds m independent copies and subtracts 1, so conditioned on survival the value can grow. Ruling this out needs an upper bound on E(X_n | X_n != 0) of order 1, which by Conjectures 1 and 3 is equivalent to the constants in those conjectures, i.e. the same missing universal constant as in D0056.
result: The geometric law with P(Y = k) proportional to m^{-k} is exactly the law whose m-tilt is uniform on Z_+ in the improper sense, i.e. the unique law making the tilting weight m^{x} constant against the law. Concretely, the conjecture says that conditionally on survival, the critical recursion converges to the law that is invariant under the m-tilt up to normalisation. This identifies the conjectured limit as a quasi-stationary law for the tilted recursion, which is the correct framework: Y_infinity should be the Yaglom limit of the recursion conditioned on non-extinction, and the geometric shape is forced by the requirement that the tilted process be a martingale. So the conjecture is a Yaglom-type limit theorem, and the two ingredients needed are (i) tightness of the conditional laws and (ii) uniqueness of the quasi-stationary law.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: E(X_n^r) = P(X_n != 0) E(X_n^r | X_n != 0); with the two conjectured inputs this gives c(r) = (4/(m-1)) sum_k k^r m^{-k}, and c(1) = 4m/(m-1)^3 as stated.
method: Combine the source's own reductions. The source shows (its Lemma 4 plus Lemma 5) that Conjecture 1 implies the E(X_n) half of Conjecture 3 without using Conjecture 2.
obstruction: The uniform integrability of X_n^r given survival is not free for large r: the conditional law is conjecturally geometric with all moments, but a priori the conditional distribution could have a heavy tail contributed by rare large values, and controlling it requires the same moment bounds as D0056. So Conjecture 3 inherits both walls.
result: The general-r half is exactly Conjectures 1 and 2 together, and saying so precisely is the content here: if P(X_n != 0) ~ 4/((m-1)^2 n^2) and the conditional law converges to the geometric law with ratio 1/m, then E(X_n^r) = P(X_n != 0) E(X_n^r | X_n != 0) tends to (4/((m-1)^2 n^2)) * sum_k k^r (m-1)/m^k = (4/((m-1) n^2)) sum_k k^r m^{-k} = c(r)/n^2, which is exactly the conjectured constant. So Conjecture 3 carries NO independent content beyond Conjectures 1 and 2 plus uniform integrability of X_n^r conditioned on survival. I verified the constant arithmetic: with r = 1, sum_k k m^{-k} = m/(m-1)^2, so c(1) = 4m/((m-1)(m-1)^2) = 4m/(m-1)^3, matching the source's stated constant. That arithmetic check is a control on my reading of the extracted formulas.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Formula (a) has a pole at s = m with residue 4m/(m-1); the crossover to the n^{-1} regime of (b) happens at m - s of order 1/n.
method: Check the internal consistency of (a) and (b) as s tends to m, which is the natural test of the conjectured constants and is not done in the source.
obstruction: The same wall as D0056: the proved Theorem 3 gives the 1/n order in (b) with initial-law-dependent constants, and identifying the universal constant needs a forgetting-of-the-initial-law argument at criticality where the linearisation has spectral radius 1.
result: The two parts are consistent in a way that explains the change of order, and verifying this is the contribution. Formula (a) has a pole at s = m with residue (4m/(m-1)^2)(m-1)/(m-s) = (4m/(m-1)) / (m-s), so as s increases to m the n^{-2} asymptotic degenerates. Matching the two regimes requires the crossover to occur when (m-s) is of order 1/n, and substituting s = m - a/n into (a) gives (4m/(m-1)^2)((m-1-a/n)/(a/n)) n^{-2} = (4m/(m-1)) /(a n) + O(n^{-2}), i.e. an n^{-1} law with an a-dependent constant. Setting a to the crossover scale a = 2m/(... ) recovers an n^{-1} term; in particular the CONJECTURED constant in (b), 2/(m-1), is not the naive s -> m limit of (a) but a genuinely new constant, so (b) is independent information. The conjectures are therefore consistent but (b) is not implied by (a).

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: All known proofs build a bounded-cost interface surface from two infinite clusters at p near 1; infinitely presented groups have no such surface.
method: Look at what the known proofs have in common. Babson-Benjamini use a finite presentation to build a cocycle/co-boundary argument showing that at p close to 1 two infinite clusters would force an infinite 'interface' surface with too much cost; the planar case uses duality; the product case uses a slab argument.
obstruction: Infinitely presented groups are the wall: for such a group every candidate surface has unbounded-length relators, so the counting bound has no uniform cost per unit area. A proof for that class would need either a new invariant replacing the presentation complex or an argument that infinitely presented one-ended nonamenable groups do not exist with the relevant geometry, which is false.
result: The unifying mechanism is that all four proofs produce, from a hypothetical pair of infinite clusters at p near 1, a surface (interface) with area much larger than its boundary, contradicting a counting bound. Finite presentation supplies the surface via relators of bounded length; planarity supplies it via the dual graph; a product supplies it via a slab. The obstruction to the general case is therefore exactly the class of one-ended transitive nonamenable graphs with NO bounded-length surface structure -- infinitely presented groups. Two structural remarks I can add: (i) one-endedness is necessary, since a tree (infinitely many ends) has p_u = 1; (ii) the conjecture is a statement at p near 1, hence a low-temperature/perturbative regime, so it should be more accessible than p_c < p_u, and the known results support that.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Nonuniqueness near p_c should follow from a branching-random-walk comparison with spectral radius < 1; the missing input is a sharp count of open self-avoiding paths.
method: Ask what quantity separates p_c and p_u. The uniqueness threshold is characterised by the vanishing of the two-point function's exponential decay in the 'touching' sense, and Schonmann's proof for large Cheeger constant compares the cluster growth with a branching random walk on the graph.
obstruction: The wall is that the number of open paths is not the number of paths times p^n: paths share edges, and the correlations between them are exactly what makes percolation hard. Every known proof of p_c < p_u either has enough geometry to bound the sharing (planarity, product structure) or enough spectral gap to absorb it (Schonmann's Cheeger condition), and neither is available in general.
result: The branching-random-walk comparison is the right frame and it identifies exactly what a general proof needs: at p slightly above p_c the cluster of the origin behaves like the range of a branching random walk with mean offspring slightly above 1, and on a nonamenable graph such a range has spectral radius strictly less than 1, hence two independent copies do not intersect and uniqueness fails. Making this rigorous needs a comparison of the cluster with a branching random walk that is valid at ALL p in a right neighbourhood of p_c, i.e. an estimate of the form: the expected number of open paths of length n from the origin grows at most like (p * branching rate)^n with the SAME exponent as the branching random walk. The source itself points to this analogy (its remark connecting Conjecture 3.8 to branching random walk and the Benjamini-Schramm Theorem 4). So the missing input is a sharp upper bound on the number of open self-avoiding paths, which is the same object as the connective constant appearing in the self-avoiding walk problems recorded here as D0066-D0077.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Smirnov's observable uses the three-colour identity special to the triangular lattice; on Z^2 the RSW theory gives tightness and now rotational invariance, but not the conformal upgrade.
method: Identify what Smirnov's proof uses that is lattice-specific. The proof builds three discrete harmonic-conjugate observables from the three colours of a hexagonal face and uses the exact combinatorial identity that a single site flip changes the three crossing events in a balanced way; the identity is special to the triangular lattice's three-fold structure.
obstruction: The wall on route (ii) is going from rotational invariance to conformal invariance: rotational invariance gives that the scaling limit is invariant under the isometry group, whereas conformal invariance requires invariance under a much larger, infinite-dimensional group, and no known argument bootstraps one to the other without an exactly holomorphic observable.
result: The known route to universality has two candidate replacements for Smirnov's observable, and stating them is the useful output. (i) A discrete-holomorphic parafermionic observable, which for the random-cluster model exists at every q and is used by Duminil-Copin and collaborators, but whose discrete holomorphicity is exact only on the isoradial/self-dual lattices and only for a specific spin; for percolation (q=1) on Z^2 the observable is not exactly discrete holomorphic. (ii) A renormalisation/RSW route: the RSW theory for bond percolation on Z^2 is complete and gives tightness of the crossing probabilities and rotational invariance up to sub-sequences, so the missing step is precisely the identification of the subsequential limits, i.e. a uniqueness statement, not an existence one. The recent proof of rotational invariance for the random-cluster model by Duminil-Copin, Kozlowski, Krachun, Manolescu and Oulamara is a big step on route (ii); full conformal invariance still needs the dilation/translation-to-conformal upgrade.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Conjectured limit N_alpha = alpha-stable subordinator jumps placed at points sampled from the derivative martingale M', the GMC analogue of the decorated Poisson point process for branching random walk.
method: Separate the two statements the conjecture bundles: convergence of the reordered atom masses (a Poisson-Dirichlet statement, known in several settings from the branching random walk literature) and convergence of the measures with their SPATIAL positions.
obstruction: The wall is the same one that makes the maximum problem hard: the log-correlated field is only approximately a branching random walk, and the error in the approximation is of the same order as the correction terms (the 3/(2 sqrt(2d)) log c term) that the conjecture asserts. Controlling the error to that precision needs a comparison at the level of the whole extremal process, not just of the maximum, and the available comparison (Kahane's convexity inequality) is one-sided and loses constants.
result: The spatial half is the genuinely open half and it can be reduced to a decorated point process statement: N_alpha should be the alpha-stable subordinator applied to the derivative martingale measure M', i.e. N_alpha(dx) = sum_i p_i delta_{x_i} where (x_i) are sampled from M'/M'(B) and (p_i) are the jumps of an independent alpha-stable subordinator. This is exactly the structure of the extremal process of branching random walk (a decorated Poisson point process with intensity the derivative martingale), so the conjecture is the GMC analogue of the Aidekon and Arguin-Bovier-Kistler description of branching random walk extremes. The transfer therefore requires a multiscale decomposition of the log-correlated field into a branching structure with a controlled error, which is exactly the modified second moment method used for the maximum.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: The star-equation is a continuous smoothing transform; the four cases correspond to the four regimes of the discrete Biggins-Kyprianou classification.
method: Recognise the star-equation as a continuous smoothing transform (a fixed-point equation for a random measure under a multiplicative cascade) and import the classification technology from the discrete smoothing transform, where the solutions of M = sum_i A_i M_i are classified by the Biggins-Kyprianou theory.
obstruction: The wall is that the continuous star-equation has no branching structure to induce on: the discrete classification uses the tree, and in the continuum the 'cascade' is only approximate, so the standard argument (analyse the Laplace exponent of the fixed point and show it satisfies a functional equation with a known solution set) requires knowing that the fixed point has finite Laplace exponent, which fails exactly in the atomic cases (3) and (4) where the measure has infinite mean.
result: The four cases match the four regimes of the discrete smoothing transform exactly, which is the structural point worth recording: alpha is the index of the stable law entering the fixed point and gamma^2 = 2d is the boundary where the multiplicative martingale degenerates. In the discrete case the classification is a theorem: the fixed points of the smoothing transform are the (possibly stable-subordinated) multiples of the additive martingale limit in the subcritical case and of the derivative martingale at the boundary. So the conjecture asserts that the continuous star-equation has no solutions beyond the discrete list, and its content is a rigidity statement. For case (1) Shamov's characterisation of subcritical GMC as the unique measure with the right Cameron-Martin shift behaviour gives the answer, so the open content is cases (2)-(4).

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: E[e^{-qG}] = E[Z^{-q/sqrt(2d)}] Gamma(1 + q/sqrt(2d)) is exactly the randomly-shifted-Gumbel form with shift log Z / sqrt(2d), Z proportional to M'.
method: Check the internal consistency of the conjectured Laplace transform, which is cheap and is a real test of the statement.
obstruction: For general d and general log-correlated kernels the wall is the same as for the two-dimensional DGFF before Bramson-Ding-Zeitouni: one needs tightness of the centred maximum with the exact 3/2 log correction, which requires a barrier/entropic-repulsion argument for a field that is only approximately branching. In dimension d >= 3 the modified second moment method still works but the comparison with a branching random walk loses the constant in front of the log unless the kernel has a good multiscale decomposition, which is assumed rather than proved for general kernels of the form (2.12) in the source.
result: The formula has the structure forced by the Gumbel-times-derivative-martingale picture, and verifying that is the contribution. If the extremal process is a decorated Poisson point process with random intensity Z e^{-sqrt(2d) u} du, where Z is proportional to the derivative martingale M', then the maximum is G = (1/sqrt(2d)) log Z + Gumbel/sqrt(2d) in the appropriate normalisation, so E[e^{-qG}] = E[Z^{-q/sqrt(2d)}] * E[e^{-q * Gumbel/sqrt(2d)}] = E[Z^{-q/sqrt(2d)}] * Gamma(1 + q/sqrt(2d)), which is exactly the conjectured product with Z = c M'([0,1]^d). So the conjecture is precisely the statement that the limit is a randomly-shifted Gumbel with shift given by the derivative chaos -- and the Gamma factor is the Gumbel's Laplace transform, a consistency check that the stated formula passes. The constant 3/(2 sqrt(2d)) in the centring is the standard Bramson correction (3/2 times the log of the scale over the exponent), also consistent.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: SLE_{8/3} is the unique conformal restriction measure with exponent 5/8; the SAW parafermionic observable is exactly divergence-free on the hexagonal lattice but its curl is not controlled.
method: Locate what is missing relative to the models where convergence to SLE is proved (percolation, Ising, LERW, UST). In every one of those the proof supplies (a) a discrete observable that is exactly or approximately discrete holomorphic and (b) a domain Markov property.
obstruction: The wall is the missing half of discrete holomorphicity for the SAW parafermionic observable, together with the absence of any a-priori tightness/RSW theory for SAW: even sub-sequential scaling limits are not known to exist, because the SAW measure has no positive association and the standard RSW arguments fail.
result: Self-avoiding walk HAS a domain Markov property in a weak, restriction-type form (the SAW measure satisfies the restriction property in the continuum, which is exactly why SLE_{8/3} is the predicted limit -- it is the unique restriction measure with the right exponent), so the missing ingredient is entirely on the observable side. The candidate observable is the parafermionic observable of Duminil-Copin and Smirnov, which for SAW on the hexagonal lattice satisfies an exact discrete relation at the critical fugacity 1/sqrt(2 + sqrt 2); that relation is what gives the connective constant of the hexagonal lattice. So the honest state is: the observable exists and is exact on the hexagonal lattice, but only its discrete divergence-free part is known, and the discrete curl (the second half of discrete holomorphicity) is not, which is exactly what is needed to identify the scaling limit.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Ratio convergence follows from a Tauberian condition on the singularity of sum sigma_n z^n at z = 1/mu; submultiplicativity alone is compatible with oscillating ratios.
method: See what the ratio limit is equivalent to. Submultiplicativity sigma_{m+n} <= sigma_m sigma_n gives sigma_n >= mu^n and sigma_n^{1/n} decreasing to mu. The ratio limit is a Tauberian upgrade and would follow from a subadditivity-with-error statement.
obstruction: The wall is that nothing is known about the analytic structure of the SAW generating function on its circle of convergence beyond the location of the singularity, and no combinatorial argument produces a ratio limit from submultiplicativity alone (there are submultiplicative sequences with oscillating ratios). On lattices where a parafermionic observable exists (hexagonal) the connective constant is known but the correction exponent is not.
result: The ratio limit is equivalent to the statement that sigma_n mu^{-n} is asymptotically 'smooth' -- precisely, if sigma_n = mu^n n^{gamma - 1} L(n) with L slowly varying and monotone-type regularity, the ratio converges. Kesten's pattern theorem gives sigma_{n+1}/sigma_n >= mu and sigma_{n+2}/sigma_n converging to mu^2 on the SUBSEQUENCE of even n in some lattices, and the classical partial result is that the ratio converges in the Cesaro sense (immediate from sigma_n^{1/n} to mu). So the honest content is that the ratio limit is a regularity statement about the correction to exponential growth, and the only lattice-independent tool available is submultiplicativity, which cannot see it. I record one genuine implication not stated in the source: the ratio limit follows immediately if the generating function sum sigma_n z^n has a unique singularity of the same modulus on |z| = 1/mu with an algebraic (rather than oscillatory) behaviour, i.e. from an aperiodicity plus Tauberian condition -- which is exactly what a proof of the conjectured gamma = 43/32 exponent would supply.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Constancy is ergodicity applied to a translation-invariant functional; existence needs a Hammersley-Welsh bridge decomposition with environment-uniform exp(o(n)) error.
method: Split the question. Constancy across vertices (given existence) is a zero-one law: the value is measurable with respect to the percolation configuration and is invariant under the translations of Z^2 restricted to the cluster, so ergodicity gives a deterministic value. Existence of the limit is a subadditive-ergodic question.
obstruction: The wall is the uniformity of the Hammersley-Welsh error in the environment: the bridge decomposition costs exp(c sqrt n) on Z^2, and on the cluster the constant c depends on the local geometry, which is unbounded (the cluster has arbitrarily long thin necks), so the error is not uniformly subexponential. Controlling it needs a renormalisation of the cluster into good blocks, and the block estimate would have to survive the SAW's self-avoidance constraint across blocks.
result: The two halves separate cleanly and only one is hard. Constancy: log sigma_n(v) is not subadditive along the cluster because concatenating two SAWs on the cluster need not give a SAW, but the QUANTITY limsup sigma_n(v)^{1/n} is a translation-invariant function of the environment, hence a.s. constant by ergodicity of Bernoulli percolation -- this is Lacoin's non-randomness and it does not need the limit to exist. Existence: the natural route is a subadditive ergodic theorem applied to the number of BRIDGES (SAWs that stay in a slab determined by their endpoints) on the cluster, since bridges do concatenate; on Z^2 the equality of the bridge and connective constants is Hammersley-Welsh, and the source's Section 6 shows the same equality on quasi-transitive graphs with a graph height function. The infinite cluster is not quasi-transitive, but it is unimodular and has an approximate height function (the coordinate), so the honest reduction is: existence of mu(v) would follow from a Hammersley-Welsh bridge decomposition valid on the cluster with a subexponential error uniform in the environment.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: The extremal case is the bridge graph B_Delta with mu = sqrt(Delta-1); the proof of Theorem 2.1 needs condition Pi, which fails when a vertex carries a parallel class of multiplicity 3 or more.
method: Trace the proof. The bound comes from sigma^F_{2n}(v) >= (Delta - 1)^n, proved by showing that every 2n-step forward-extendable SAW has at least n(Delta - 2) extendable pairs (x,e), subject to a condition Pi; the theorem's cases are exactly the cases where Pi is verified.
obstruction: The wall is proving extremality of B_Delta without condition Pi. The natural route -- a Fisher-transformation or an entropy comparison with the bridge graph -- needs a monotonicity of mu under the operation of merging parallel edges, and the source's Section 4 shows mu is strictly monotone under ADDING edges but says nothing about redistributing multiplicities at fixed degree.
result: Condition Pi is a local statement about the multigraph and the obstruction for Delta >= 5 is combinatorial, not conceptual. In a non-simple multigraph an extendable pair (x,e) can fail to give a NEW walk when e is parallel to an edge already used, and the number of parallel classes at a vertex is what controls the loss. For Delta <= 4 a vertex has at most two parallel classes of multiplicity >= 2 and the loss can be absorbed; for Delta >= 5 there can be a parallel class of multiplicity 3 or more, and the counting of extendable pairs double counts. I record the following reduction: the bound mu >= sqrt(Delta-1) for non-simple transitive multigraphs is equivalent to the same bound for the associated SIMPLE graph with edge multiplicities, where a walk crossing a multi-edge of multiplicity k has k choices; the generating function then has a k-fold weight and the extremal case is the 'bridge graph' B_Delta for which the source records mu(B_Delta) = sqrt(Delta - 1) exactly. So the conjecture is that B_Delta is extremal in every degree, and the case Delta <= 4 is the verified part.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: sqrt(Delta - 1) <= mu_min(Delta); at Delta = 3 the conjectured value is the golden mean, giving a constant phi/sqrt 2 = 1.144 over the general bound.
method: Test candidate extremisers and see what asymptotic they force. The known general lower bound is mu >= sqrt(Delta - 1) (Theorem 2.1) and the conjectured value at Delta = 3 is the golden mean phi = 1.618..., against sqrt(2) = 1.414.
obstruction: The wall is that mu_min is an infimum over an uncountable class with no compactness: the Babai metric on rooted graphs makes G_Delta compact, but mu is not continuous on it -- that lack of continuity is exactly the locality problem of Question 7.1 (D0075 here). So one cannot even assert that the infimum is attained.
result: The candidate extremiser at Delta = 3 identified in the Grimmett-Li work is a specific 3-regular graph whose connective constant is the golden mean; the golden mean arises as the growth rate of the Fibonacci recursion counting SAWs on a ladder-like cubic graph. Extrapolating that mechanism to general Delta, the natural candidate extremiser is the 'ladder' obtained by taking a cycle-of-cliques structure of degree Delta, whose SAW counting satisfies a linear recursion with growth rate the largest root of a degree-Delta polynomial. This predicts mu_min(Delta) = Delta - 1 - c + o(1) for large Delta only if the extremiser is close to the tree, which it is not; the honest prediction from the sqrt(Delta-1) bound and the golden-mean value at Delta = 3 is that mu_min(Delta) grows like sqrt(Delta) up to constants, i.e. that the bound sqrt(Delta - 1) has the right ORDER, with the constant improving from 1 (bridge graphs) to phi/sqrt 2 = 1.144 at Delta = 3 for simple graphs. Whether the constant tends to a limit as Delta grows is the second half of the question and I have no candidate.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: With a graph height function the bridge constant equals mu and cubic bridge counting gives the Fibonacci recursion with growth phi; the conjecture reduces to the existence of a height function.
method: Ask why the golden mean and not sqrt 2. The golden mean is the growth rate of the number of binary strings with no two consecutive equal symbols in a suitable coding, and it appears as the connective constant of a specific cubic graph, so the conjecture says that graph is extremal.
obstruction: The wall is that a transitive cubic graph whose group has trivial first Betti number and infinitely many ends need not admit a height function -- the natural candidates are Cayley graphs of infinite torsion groups with three generators (Grigorchuk-type), for which no surjection onto Z exists and no Lipschitz harmonic function is known. The 2026 preprint on connective constants of Grigorchuk graphs found in the status search is presumably attacking exactly this case, and I did not fetch it.
result: The two solved regimes suggest the correct general mechanism, and naming it is the contribution. Both the positive-first-Betti-number case and the two-ended case work by producing a graph height function (respectively from a surjection onto Z coming from the abelianisation, and from a Lipschitz harmonic function). Given a graph height function the source's own bridge theory (Section 6) gives mu = the bridge constant, and the bridge counting on a cubic graph with a height function yields the Fibonacci recursion and hence phi. So the conjecture reduces to: EVERY infinite transitive cubic simple graph carries a graph height function (possibly after passing to a quotient). That reduction is exactly the programme the source describes in Sections 7-8, and it converts a counting conjecture into a group-theoretic existence statement.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: G_A transitive iff the A-orbits form a Gamma-invariant block system; if A acts freely the block system is regular and its kernel is normal.
method: This is a pure group/graph-theory question underlying the strict-inequality theorems for quotients. Ask whether transitivity of the quotient forces a normal structure.
obstruction: Turning the finite intuition into an infinite graph example requires exhibiting an infinite transitive graph with an imprimitivity system whose block kernel is not realisable as a normal subgroup of any transitive overgroup of Aut(G), and one must range over ALL transitively acting Gamma', including Aut(G) itself, which is a large and hard-to-control group. That quantification over all overgroups is the wall.
result: The relevant standard fact is that G_A is transitive if and only if Gamma acts transitively on the set of A-orbits, i.e. A's orbit partition is Gamma-invariant, which is equivalent to A being contained in a subgroup whose orbit partition is a Gamma-congruence -- and a block system for a transitive group is exactly the orbit partition of a subgroup that is normalised by a point stabiliser, NOT necessarily normal in Gamma. So the honest statement is: transitivity of G_A forces the orbits of A to form a Gamma-invariant block system, and the question becomes whether every block system of a transitive group arises from a normal subgroup of SOME transitive overgroup. For finite permutation groups the answer is negative in general (imprimitive groups with non-normal block stabilisers exist), which strongly suggests a positive answer to the source's question; the free-action hypothesis is what would make the block system regular, and for regular block systems the block stabiliser IS the kernel of the action on blocks, hence normal.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: mu(G_A) >= mu(G) always; strictness needs a proper internal pattern of G_A that does not lift, and the known sufficient condition is a new cycle length.
method: Recall why quotienting increases the count. In G_A a SAW may use a cycle that lifts to a non-closed path, so sigma_n(G_A) >= sigma_n(G) always and mu(G_A) >= mu(G); the strictness needs a quantitative gain, i.e. a positive density of walks in G_A that do not lift.
obstruction: The wall is that the pattern theorem gives a gain in the number of walks CONTAINING the pattern, but to beat mu(G) one needs the gain to survive the comparison with the lift, and without normality there is no canonical lifting map: the fibre of G -> G_A is an A-orbit but the covering is not regular unless A is normal in a group acting transitively upstairs. Building the injection from walks in G into walks in G_A that misses a positive-density set requires that regularity.
result: The known proof for normal A produces the gain by exhibiting a specific short cycle in G_A that does not lift, then applying a pattern theorem to say a positive density of walks uses it. That is exactly the stated extra condition. So the general question is whether a free action with transitive quotient always creates a NEW cycle length. It does create new cycles (any non-trivial A gives a closed walk in G_A lifting to a path from v to av), so the issue is only whether the new cycles can all have lengths that already occur in G. I record the following reduction: strictness follows from the pattern theorem as soon as G_A contains a cycle C such that the set of walks in G_A traversing C has positive density -- which by Kesten's pattern theorem holds as soon as C is a PROPER INTERNAL PATTERN of G_A, i.e. can be repeated arbitrarily often. A new cycle of a length already occurring in G is still a new pattern if the local structure differs, so the length condition in the known theorem is sufficient but far from necessary.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Question 4.10 follows from Question 4.11; failing that, a pattern-theorem argument works unless the added edges cannot be used repeatedly in a single SAW.
method: Examine the role of normality in the proof of Theorem 4.7. The proof constructs, from a SAW in G', a SAW in G by removing the new edges, and controls the entropy cost by a quasi-transitive averaging over the orbits of A; normality is used to make the orbit structure compatible with the transitive Gamma-action so that the averaging is uniform.
obstruction: The wall is that quasi-transitivity of A alone bounds the number of orbits but not the geometry within an orbit, so the added edges can be arranged (in principle) so that using two of them in the same SAW is impossible; ruling that out is where the normality or finite-index hypothesis enters.
result: The source itself points to the right repair, in its Question 4.11: normality can be dispensed with if there is a transitive Gamma containing A with Gamma intersect Stab_v contained in A. That is precisely the condition making the orbit-averaging uniform, so Question 4.10 follows from Question 4.11, and the honest content of this attempt is the confirmation that the two questions are linked in that direction (the source asserts the implication; I checked it is the averaging step that needs it). Beyond that, a direct route avoiding both: since the added edges are A-invariant and A is quasi-transitive, the density of new edges along a walk is bounded below by a constant depending only on the number of A-orbits, so a pattern-theorem argument applies to the new edge as a pattern and gives mu(G') > mu(G) PROVIDED the new edge can be repeated arbitrarily often in a SAW, which holds unless the new edges form a set of bounded 'reach'. So the residual case is augmentations by edges that cannot be used repeatedly.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: The condition says Gamma has no stabiliser beyond A, so existence is a group-extension problem with obstruction class in H^2(orbit group, A).
method: Read the condition Gamma intersect Stab_v <= A as saying that Gamma is 'no bigger than A on stabilisers', i.e. Gamma is generated by A together with elements moving the base point, with no extra local symmetry.
obstruction: Computing the obstruction requires knowing Aut(G), and for a general quasi-transitive graph Aut(G) is a topological group whose structure is not determined by the combinatorics; there is no algorithm even to decide transitivity of a given subgroup in general. That is the wall.
result: The condition is exactly that Gamma acts on G with A as the stabiliser of the A-orbit partition and with a FREE action on the orbit space, so the question asks when a quasi-transitive action extends to a transitive action with no new point stabilisers. A necessary condition is that the A-orbits all have the same 'local type', since Gamma must map orbits to orbits isomorphically; this is a finite check when A has finitely many orbits. A sufficient condition in the finitely generated case: if the orbit space carries a free transitive action of some group H and the extension problem for the pair (A, H) has a solution (i.e. the relevant group cohomology class in H^2(H, A) is the one realised by the graph), then Gamma exists. So the answer is governed by a group-extension obstruction, which is the structural output of this attempt.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: mu is upper semicontinuous in the Babai metric; locality fails only from below, and a graph height function supplies the missing local lower bound via bridges.
method: Test the naive statement. Locality cannot hold without hypotheses: the connective constant of a large-girth graph can be far from that of a tree with the same local structure, in the same way that p_c is not local without a growth hypothesis.
obstruction: Removing the height function needs a bridge decomposition (or some other way to make mu an infimum of local quantities) valid without it; mu is a limsup of local counts and is upper semicontinuous in the Babai metric, so the only failure is from below, i.e. one needs a matching lower bound from local data, which is exactly what a height function provides.
result: The natural obstruction is uniform amenability, and identifying it is the content here. Take G_n a sequence of graphs that look like the 3-regular tree in balls of radius n but are globally amenable (for example a large-girth 3-regular Cayley graph of a finite group, made infinite by a suitable limit). Then K(G, G_n) tends to infinity with G the tree and mu(G) = 2, while mu(G_n) can be strictly smaller because the global structure forces walks to return. This is the graph-counting analogue of the failure of locality for p_c on amenable graphs, and it shows that any general condition must exclude such sequences -- exactly what the graph-height-function hypothesis of Theorem 8.1 does, by supplying a uniform bridge decomposition. So the honest conjecture is: locality holds along sequences carrying graph height functions with UNIFORMLY BOUNDED parameters (d, r), and the source's Theorem proves a version of this; the open part is whether the uniform bound can be relaxed to a growth or non-amenability condition.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Nachmias-Peres: (Delta-1) rho < mu compares SAW entropy with the return cost; it fails when mu is much below Delta - 1.
method: Understand the Nachmias-Peres condition. Bounding the number of SAWs by the number of non-backtracking walks gives an entropy of (Delta-1)^n against a return probability rho^n; when (Delta-1) rho < mu the entropy of SAWs exceeds the cost of returning, so walks that return are exponentially rare and the speed is positive.
obstruction: The wall is that the number of SAWs of length n staying within distance eps n of the origin is not known to be exponentially smaller than sigma_n on a general nonamenable graph; proving this is a large-deviation statement for SAW which currently requires the same entropy comparison. A route through the (unproved) equality of bridge and connective constants on all quasi-transitive graphs -- which needs a graph height function, exactly the object missing in Question 3.4 and 7.1 -- is available for graphs that carry one.
result: The condition is exactly an entropy-versus-return comparison, and the honest statement of the gap is that it can fail even for very nonamenable graphs. Since mu <= Delta - 1 always, the condition (Delta-1) rho < mu requires rho < mu/(Delta-1) <= 1, so it is a quantitative nonamenability requirement, and it fails when mu is much smaller than Delta - 1, i.e. for graphs with many short cycles (girth 3 with many triangles) even if rho is small. So the residual class is: nonamenable graphs with small connective constant relative to degree. For those, the free-energy/bridge route is more promising: on a nonamenable transitive graph the bridge generating function should have a strictly positive radius gap, and positive speed would follow from an exponential bound on the number of SAWs returning to a ball of radius eps n.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Peanosphere convergence determines (mu_h, eta) modulo embedding; the embedded statement needs no macroscopic faces plus an up-to-constants modulus of continuity.
method: Separate the conjecture into the two things it asserts: that the embedded map has a scaling limit at all (tightness), and that the limit is the sqrt 2-LQG measure of a quantum cone.
obstruction: The wall is the same polylogarithmic loss as in D0050: the strong coupling with Brownian motion controls graph distances and Dirichlet energies only up to polylogarithmic factors, whereas the modulus of continuity of a conformal embedding needs up-to-constants control. The Cardy-embedding proof avoided this by using percolation observables instead of distances, and the corresponding observable for the spanning-tree model is the Mullin walk itself, which is why the circle-packing route in the flagged seminar lead is plausible.
result: Tightness under a conformal embedding is the hard half and it has a known reduction: the family of embedded area measures is tight as soon as one has (a) an upper bound on the maximal face diameter (no macroscopic faces, Problem 6.6 of the source, recorded here as D0085) and (b) a bound on the modulus of continuity of the embedding, both of which are consequences of up-to-constants estimates for the discrete Dirichlet energy. Given tightness, identification of the limit as exp(sqrt 2 h) follows from the mating-of-trees theorem plus the fact that the encoding walk converges to correlated Brownian motion, since the peanosphere topology determines the pair (measure, curve) modulo the embedding. So the conjecture is exactly 'peanosphere convergence plus tightness implies embedded convergence', which is the general programme of Sections 5.2-5.3 of the source.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: For gamma = sqrt 2 the mating-of-trees Brownian motion has independent coordinates; the conjectured independence of (mu_h, eta) is the continuum shadow of that.
method: Ask why the limits are independent when the discrete objects are not, since that is the surprising part and any proof must explain it.
obstruction: The conditional law of the Peano curve given the map is not accessible: conditioning on the map is conditioning the walk on a complicated functional (the map is the walk modulo the bijection's equivalence), and no description of that conditional law is known. This is the discrete face of the same difficulty as Problem 6.4 (two independent decorations, D0082 here).
result: The independence is a consequence of the mating-of-trees theorem read backwards, and stating it explains what a proof needs. In the continuum, (h, eta) is a measurable function of the two-sided correlated Brownian motion Z, and for kappa = 8 (gamma = sqrt 2) the two coordinates of Z are INDEPENDENT; the field h is a function of the pair through a symmetric functional while the curve eta is determined by the whole path, and the independence of (mu_h, eta) is the statement that the field-valued and curve-valued functionals of Z are independent. So a proof of Conjecture 3.2 must supply the discrete counterpart: the conditional law of the discrete Peano curve given the map must converge to the law of eta, which is exactly the claim the source makes in its own justification. That reduces the conjecture to a conditional-convergence statement for the Mullin walk given the map, i.e. to a mixing statement for the walk conditioned on its 'tree-shape'.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: i.i.d. increments correspond to a bijection with an unconstrained word in a free monoid; nonlocal decoration constraints destroy it.
method: Ask what forces i.i.d. increments. In the Mullin and Kenyon-Miller-Sheffield-Wilson bijections the walk increments are i.i.d. because the decorated map is built by a sequence of independent local choices; in the hamburger-cheeseburger bijection the walk is a stack-based process and its increments depend on the history.
obstruction: For a decoration whose local exploration is not deterministic-given-the-past (which is the case whenever the model has a nonlocal constraint such as acyclicity or connectivity), the encoding word is constrained and the increments are dependent. Constructing a bijection means finding a local rule that resolves the nonlocal constraint, and that is exactly the art of bijective combinatorics; there is no general method.
result: The structural criterion is that the bijection be a 'free' encoding: the decorated map corresponds to an unconstrained word in a free monoid, so that the uniform measure on maps pulls back to a product measure on letters. Mullin (words in a 4-letter alphabet with a balanced-parenthesis constraint that becomes a walk), bipolar orientations (Kenyon-Miller-Sheffield-Wilson, walks in the quarter plane with i.i.d. steps) and Schnyder woods are of this type. The hamburger-cheeseburger encoding is not, because the burger stack introduces a memory. So the search for new i.i.d. bijections is the search for further decorated-map classes in bijection with an unconstrained lattice walk, and the natural candidates are decorations by other spanning structures with a local exploration rule (for instance Eulerian orientations, or spanning forests with a fixed number of components).

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: The hamburger-cheeseburger walk is a functional of i.i.d. letters with exponentially decaying memory: Berkes-Liu-Wu gives an n^{1/4+eps} strong coupling, Theorem 5.1 needs n^{o(1)}.
method: Identify the minimal coupling strength needed. Theorem 5.1 of the source compares the map with the mated-CRT map through a strong coupling of the encoding walk with Brownian motion; the source suggests either proving a strong coupling for the hamburger-cheeseburger walk or finding a route that works with a weaker coupling.
obstruction: The wall is therefore quantitative: an n^{1/4} almost-sure invariance principle is available for the hamburger-cheeseburger walk but Theorem 5.1 needs n^{o(1)}. Improving the invariance principle to n^{o(1)} for a stack functional with exponential memory is not known and would be of independent interest.
result: The second route is the more promising and can be made precise. The hamburger-cheeseburger walk is a function of an i.i.d. sequence of letters through a stack (a queue-like transformation), so it is a deterministic functional of an i.i.d. sequence with unbounded but exponentially decaying memory (the burger stack's relevant depth has exponential tails at criticality). A strong coupling theorem for such 'functionals of i.i.d. with exponentially decaying memory' does exist in the literature for MARTINGALE approximations (Berkes-Liu-Wu), giving an almost sure invariance principle with error n^{1/4+eps}. That error is worse than KMT's log n but still o(n^{1/2}), and the honest question is whether Theorem 5.1 can be run with an n^{1/4+eps} coupling error rather than a polylogarithmic one. My reading of the proof structure is that it cannot, because the comparison of graph distances requires the coupling error to be smaller than the smallest scale at which the mated-CRT map is compared, which is polynomial only if the exponents are favourable.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: c = -4 gives Q = sqrt(29/6) = 2.1985 and gamma = 1.2856; the original conjecture's correlation -cos(pi gamma^2/4) = -0.269, while two independent SLE_8 curves give correlation 0.
method: Take the correction seriously and ask what the c = -4 prediction changes. Central charge c = -4 corresponds to gamma with 25 - 6(2/gamma + gamma/2)^2 = -4, and the decoration is by two INDEPENDENT SLE_8 curves rather than by a curve matched to gamma.
obstruction: The wall for the convergence statement itself is that the meander walk is defined through a matching of two independent arch systems, so it is a functional of two independent Dyck-path-like objects with a nonlocal pairing; no invariance principle for such a pairing is known, and the pairing is what produces the (now expected zero) correlation.
result: The arithmetic of the corrected prediction is checkable and I checked it: c = -4 gives (2/gamma + gamma/2)^2 = 29/6, so Q = sqrt(29/6) = 2.1985, and solving gamma/2 + 2/gamma = Q gives gamma^2 - 2 Q gamma + 4 = 0, gamma = Q - sqrt(Q^2 - 4) = 2.1985 - sqrt(0.8333) = 2.1985 - 0.9129 = 1.2856. With that gamma, the ORIGINAL conjectured correlation -cos(pi gamma^2/4) = -cos(pi * 0.4132) = -cos(1.2981) = -0.2691, whereas two independent SLE_8 curves correspond to a pair of independent Brownian motions, i.e. correlation 0. So the correction is not a small adjustment of the constant but a change of the whole structure, and the honest content of this row is that the numerical value in the source's conjecture is superseded while the convergence statement (Z converges to a two-dimensional Brownian motion) is not.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Problem 6.4 is the statement that the asymptotic common information of (M,P_1) and (M,P_2) is the limiting LQG surface.
method: Ask what the obstacle is, given that the marginal convergences are assumed. The walks Z_1 and Z_2 do not separate the randomness of the map from that of the decoration, so their joint law is not determined by the two marginals plus 'independence of the decorations'.
obstruction: Common information does not pass to weak limits in general -- two sequences of pairs can converge jointly while their common sigma-fields converge to something strictly smaller than the common sigma-field of the limit. Ruling this out needs a quantitative statement that the map is measurably reconstructible from each decorated walk with a vanishing error, which is exactly what the percolation proof supplies through the metric-and-peanosphere joint convergence and which is unavailable in general.
result: The correct formulation is a conditional-independence statement and identifying it is the useful step: what must be shown is that, conditionally on the LIMITING surface, the two limiting curves are independent, i.e. that the sigma-field generated by the surface is exactly the intersection of the sigma-fields generated by the two decorated pairs. In the discrete setting the map is the common information of (M,P_1) and (M,P_2), and the statement is that common information is asymptotically the surface. So Problem 6.4 is a discrete-to-continuum statement about COMMON INFORMATION, which is a different kind of object from a scaling limit and explains why it is not immediate from Theorem 4.6.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Tutte embedding is controlled by Dirichlet energies (which transfer up to polylogs); the residual obstacle is the maximal face size, a distance-type quantity.
method: Ask which embedding requires only polylogarithmic control. The Tutte embedding is defined by harmonic functions, so it is controlled by Dirichlet energies rather than by distances, and Dirichlet energies are exactly what Theorem 5.1 transfers.
obstruction: The wall is that a polylogarithmic distortion of the Dirichlet form does NOT control the maximal face size, which is a distance-type quantity, and a Tutte embedding with macroscopic faces does not converge to a measure at all. So Problem 6.5 for the Tutte embedding reduces to Problem 6.6, exactly as the source suggests.
result: The right target is therefore the Tutte (or Smith) embedding rather than the uniformizing map, and this is a genuine narrowing of the problem: Gwynne-Miller-Sheffield proved Tutte-embedding convergence for the mated-CRT map itself, and Theorem 5.1 transfers Dirichlet energies up to polylogarithmic factors. A harmonic embedding is stable under a polylogarithmic distortion of the Dirichlet form in the sense that the embedded vertex positions move by a polylogarithmic factor in the energy norm, and convergence in the vague topology of the area measure requires only that this movement be o(1) at macroscopic scales. So the honest assessment is that the polylogarithmic loss may be tolerable for the Tutte embedding, and the real obstruction is elsewhere: the absence of macroscopic faces (Problem 6.6, D0085).

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: For a Tutte embedding, a macroscopic face has harmonic measure bounded below, and harmonic measure is a resistance (Dirichlet-energy) quantity that Theorem 5.1 transfers.
method: Look for a formulation of 'no macroscopic faces' as an energy quantity, since energies are what Theorem 5.1 transfers.
obstruction: The gap in the argument above is that the correspondence 'macroscopic face iff bounded-below harmonic measure' requires the embedding to be the Tutte embedding (where harmonic measure and the embedding are directly linked) and a control of the face's boundary length; a face with a very long boundary can have small harmonic measure per boundary vertex and still be macroscopic. Making the equivalence quantitative needs a bound on the maximal face degree in the map, which for spanning-tree-weighted maps has a heavy tail. That heavy tail is the wall.
result: There is one, and it is the useful output. A face of the embedded map is macroscopic exactly when the harmonic measure from infinity of that face is bounded below, equivalently when the effective resistance from the face's boundary cycle to a macroscopic annulus is bounded above. Effective resistance IS a Dirichlet-energy quantity (it is the reciprocal of the minimal energy of a unit flow), so 'no macroscopic faces' can be phrased as: for every eps, the maximum over faces of the harmonic measure of the face tends to zero -- a statement about resistances, which Theorem 5.1 transfers up to polylogarithmic factors. This converts the problem into a resistance estimate for the mated-CRT map, uniform over faces, and the polylogarithmic loss is harmless because the target is a qualitative 'tends to zero' with polynomial decay available on the mated-CRT side.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Genus-g encoding should be boundary-length processes on a ribbon graph with matching conditions; the random modulus is then a functional of those processes, but mapping-class-group equivariance is not automatic.
method: Ask what has to be added to the simply-connected theory. Mating of trees encodes a simply-connected surface decorated by a space-filling curve by a two-dimensional correlated Brownian motion; on a surface of genus g the space-filling curve is still defined but the encoding must record the topology.
obstruction: The wall is that the decomposition is not canonical: different pants decompositions give different encodings and the consistency (mapping class group equivariance) of the resulting law on moduli space is not automatic. In the path-integral approach the law on moduli space is postulated (the DDK ansatz); deriving it from the discrete side requires exactly the equivariance that the encoding does not manifestly have.
result: The natural encoding is a Brownian motion on a graph rather than on the line, and saying so is the structural output. A space-filling exploration of a genus-g decorated map returns to previously visited regions in a way recorded by the surface's fundamental group, so the encoding object should be a pair of boundary-length processes indexed by the edges of a ribbon graph (a pair of pants decomposition), with a matching condition at each vertex of the decomposition. The moduli of the surface then appear as the (random) lengths of the decomposition curves, which are functionals of the encoding process -- giving a candidate description of the random modulus as a functional of correlated Brownian motions on a graph. That is the concrete programme this attempt produces.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Matching kappa = gamma^2 or 16/gamma^2 makes the two cut surfaces independent and Z Levy; mismatched parameters should give a Markov-additive Z with a discrepancy state variable.
method: Ask what the matching condition kappa = gamma^2 or 16/gamma^2 does. It is exactly the condition under which the SLE curve is the interface of a conformal welding of two INDEPENDENT quantum wedges, which is what makes Z a Levy-type process.
obstruction: Testing it requires computing a two-point function of the LQG measure across an SLE_kappa with mismatched kappa, and the only tool for such computations -- the imaginary-geometry coupling of SLE with the GFF -- has its own matching condition between kappa and the field's coupling constant, so it does not apply. That is the wall.
result: For mismatched parameters the pair of cut surfaces is dependent, so the boundary length process has memory; the honest reformulation is that Z should be a Markov process in a LARGER state space that records the conditional law of one side given the other. The natural candidate for that state space is the pair (boundary length, a 'field-decoration' variable measuring the discrepancy between kappa and gamma^2), and the discrepancy variable should evolve autonomously as a diffusion whose drift is proportional to (kappa - gamma^2). This predicts that Z is a Markov ADDITIVE process (a Markov-modulated Levy process) rather than a Levy process, which is a concrete and testable structure.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Mating of trees is a statement about the quantum area and boundary measures, which do not exist for c in (1,25); a metric-based reformulation is needed.
method: Check which ingredients of the theory survive when the area measure does not exist. Mating of trees encodes a surface by the boundary lengths of the space-filling curve's past and future, and boundary length is defined through the quantum boundary measure.
obstruction: The wall is that the supercritical LQG metric has infinitely many singular points (the metric is not a length metric in the naive sense and there is a dense set of points at infinite distance), so a space-filling curve parametrised by metric length may not exist. Establishing the existence of such a parametrisation is a prerequisite that has not been addressed.
result: The obstruction is precise and worth stating: the mating-of-trees encoding is a statement about MEASURES (the two boundary-length processes and the area they enclose), and in the c in (1,25) phase there is no canonical area or boundary measure, only a metric. So a mating-of-trees theory there must be re-founded on a metric quantity -- the natural candidate being the LQG distance to the curve, or the quantum natural time of the space-filling curve replaced by its metric length. This suggests the correct object is a 'mating of trees in the metric', encoding a supercritical surface by the two metric-boundary processes of a space-filling exploration. That reformulation is the output of this attempt.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: The quantum welding homeomorphism matches the two boundary measures; it is Holder but fails quasisymmetry exactly at the boundary thick points.
method: Recall the classical analytic criteria for conformal welding: a welding homeomorphism that is quasisymmetric welds uniquely (Beurling-Ahlfors), and more generally a homeomorphism in the Weil-Petersson class or satisfying a Beltrami-solvability condition welds. So the question is what regularity class the quantum welding homeomorphism belongs to.
obstruction: No such welding theorem is known. Existence for non-quasisymmetric welding maps is genuinely delicate (there are homeomorphisms that do not weld at all), and uniqueness fails without conformal removability of the image curve, which is a property of the interface, not of the data. That is the wall the source itself names.
result: The welding homeomorphism for two independent quantum wedges is the map matching quantum boundary lengths, i.e. the composition of one boundary measure's distribution function with the inverse of the other's. Both are (multifractal) measures with a known multifractal spectrum, so the homeomorphism's Holder regularity can be read off: it is Holder continuous with exponents given by the ratio of the boundary-measure exponents, but it is NOT quasisymmetric (the boundary measures have thick points where the local dimension degenerates), which is exactly why the classical criteria fail. That identification -- the welding map is Holder but not quasisymmetric, with the failure concentrated on the boundary thick points -- is the concrete content of this attempt and it tells one which analytic criterion would have to be developed: a welding theorem for homeomorphisms that are quasisymmetric off a set of Hausdorff dimension zero.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Welding map = F_2^{-1} o F_1 with F_i the gamma_i boundary-measure distribution functions; for gamma_1 != gamma_2 the multifractal exponents do not cancel and the local Holder exponent is unbounded in both directions.
method: Compute the regularity of the welding homeomorphism in the mismatched case, using the multifractal spectra of the two boundary measures, and compare with the matched case.
obstruction: With the welding map failing Holder continuity, even existence is in doubt, and no known welding theorem applies. The wall is that the two fields are independent, so their thick points do not align, and there is no reason for the composed map to be regular anywhere.
result: The mismatched case is STRICTLY worse and quantifying that is the useful output. The gamma-LQG boundary measure has quantum-length exponents governed by the parameter gamma, and the welding map is F_2^{-1} composed with F_1 where F_i is the distribution function of the gamma_i boundary measure. In the matched case gamma_1 = gamma_2 the two measures have the same multifractal spectrum and the exponents cancel on the diagonal of the spectrum, so the map is Holder with exponent bounded away from 0 and 1 on a full-measure set. When gamma_1 != gamma_2 the spectra do not cancel: at a point that is alpha-thick for the first field and typical for the second, the local Holder exponent is the ratio of two different exponents and is unbounded above and below as alpha ranges, so the welding map has points of infinite and of zero local Holder exponent. Consequently the welding map is NOT Holder on any set of full measure, which is a strictly stronger failure of regularity than in the matched case and predicts that the interface, if it exists, is not a curve of finite dimension in the usual sense.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: zeta_c is monotone hence has at most countably many jumps; the possible failure is a left discontinuity, and strictness reduces to the odometer having positive density in the fixating phase.
method: Ask which of the two properties is soft. Monotonicity is proved by a coupling in which increasing lambda makes particles fall asleep more readily; strictness needs the coupling to be strictly improving with positive probability, and continuity is a statement about the absence of a jump.
obstruction: The wall for both is that zeta_c is defined through an infinite-volume fixation event with no known continuity in the parameters other than via monotonicity; there is no variational formula for zeta_c that could be differentiated, and every known bound (zeta_c >= lambda/(1+lambda), zeta_c < 1) is proved by a different technique with different constants, so they cannot be pieced together into a modulus of continuity.
result: Continuity from one side is free and worth recording: zeta_c is non-decreasing, so it has left and right limits everywhere and at most countably many jumps, and by the definition of zeta_c as an infimum over densities at which the system stays active, zeta_c is upper semicontinuous in lambda if the fixation event is monotone and closed under increasing limits of lambda. So the only possible failure is a downward jump, i.e. left-discontinuity. Strict monotonicity: the coupling that proves Theorem 2.14 replaces each sleep attempt by a stronger one, and the gain per attempt is bounded below by a constant times (lambda' - lambda)/(1+lambda'), so a strict gain follows as soon as one shows that the number of sleep attempts before fixation is of order the volume, which is exactly a statement that the odometer is of positive density -- available in the fixating phase.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: E[m(0)] < infinity implies E[T] = n E[m(0)] = O(n) on the cycle, which is stronger than the n log^2 n bound of (6.3).
method: Read the dichotomy as a finite-size signature of the infinite-volume phase. Above the critical curve the infinite system stays active, which should force exponentially many topplings on the cycle; below it the system fixates, which should force n polylog n.
obstruction: The wall is E[m(0)] < infinity: it is NOT known in the whole fixating phase (that is D0097 below), and without it the finite-volume odometer can have a heavy tail that makes the mean diverge while the odometer is a.s. finite. So the dichotomy is entangled with the moment problem for the odometer.
result: One direction has a clean reduction and it is the useful part. If the infinite system with density zeta and rate lambda fixates a.s., then the odometer at the origin is a.s. finite; if in addition E[m(0)] < infinity (which the source records as known for zeta < zeta_c under conditions -- see D0097), then by translation invariance the expected total odometer on the cycle is n E[m(0)] = O(n), and Markov's inequality gives P(T <= C n / delta) >= 1 - delta, which is stronger than the stated n log^2 n bound. So the fast half of the dichotomy follows from finiteness of the mean odometer, and the source's own log^2 n bound is a weaker statement proved without it. The slow half (exponential T in the active phase) needs a lower bound on the time to stabilise, which follows from a supercritical percolation-type argument on the cycle.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: T <= kappa n without logs is equivalent to a uniform polynomial upper tail for the site odometer in the fast phase.
method: Locate where the two logarithms come from in the source's proof. The cyclic toppling procedure of Section 6.1 stabilises the cycle in rounds; each round costs a log from a union bound over sites and a second log from the number of rounds needed for the alive/steady labelling to settle.
obstruction: No tail bound for the odometer in the fast phase is known beyond finiteness under strong conditions, and the odometer is a global functional (it is determined by the whole configuration through abelianness), so local arguments do not produce tails. That is the wall.
