result: The linear-in-n target is exactly E[T] = n E[m(0)] with the odometer having a finite mean and, for a high-probability statement, an exponential or at least polynomial tail. So removing the logs is equivalent to an upper tail bound P(m(0) > t) <= t^{-(1+eps)} uniform in n, and the two logarithms in the source's bound are the price of a crude union bound over sites and rounds rather than a genuine tail estimate. This identifies the improvement as a tail problem for the odometer, not as a refinement of the toppling procedure.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Box odometers in Z^d increase to the infinite-volume odometer, giving tightness; the cycle is a quotient, so the monotone comparison fails.
method: Compare the finite-volume odometer with the infinite-volume one. On Z^d the odometer m(0) of the stabilisation of the whole lattice is a.s. finite in the fixating phase; tightness on the cycle is the statement that the finite-volume odometers do not blow up as n grows.
obstruction: On the cycle the total number of particles is conserved, so there is no comparison with an infinite system that has an escape route; the wall is that no monotone coupling exists between the cycle of size n and the cycle of size 2n.
result: Tightness follows from the abelian property plus a monotone approximation, provided the finite-volume stabilisation can be dominated by the infinite-volume one. The abelian property gives that stabilising the cycle is the same as stabilising in any order, and stabilising a larger region only increases the odometer at the origin (monotonicity of the odometer in the domain), so on Z^d the finite-box odometers increase to the infinite-volume odometer, and tightness follows from its a.s. finiteness. The difficulty specific to the CYCLE is that it is not an increasing family of subsets of Z: the cycle Z_n is a quotient, not a subgraph, so the monotone approximation does not apply and mass cannot leave. So the honest statement is that tightness is immediate for boxes in Z^d and is genuinely open only for the cyclic (conservative) boundary condition, which is the setting of Theorem 6.1.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: The slow-phase proof uses the linear order of the cycle; a bias supplies a drift that should preserve it, but no ordering exists for d >= 2.
method: Ask what breaks in the source's proof. The slow-phase bound (6.2) is proved on the one-dimensional cycle by a cyclic toppling procedure that exploits the linear order of the sites; the fast-phase bound (6.3) uses a comparison with a one-dimensional queueing/interface argument.
obstruction: For d >= 2 the wall is the absence of an ordering-based toppling procedure; every known proof of an exponential lower bound on T uses the one-dimensional structure to propagate activity along a line, and in higher dimensions activity can be trapped in a bounded region without a comparable cost.
result: For biased jumps in d = 1 the slow-phase argument should be EASIER, not harder: a bias makes the walkers transient, the active phase is larger (Theorem 7.2 of the source is proved for transient walks), and the cyclic procedure only needs a positive drift of the alive front, which the bias supplies. So my expectation is that the biased d = 1 case is accessible with the existing method. In d >= 2 the difficulty is different in kind: the cyclic toppling procedure has no analogue because there is no linear order, and the natural substitute -- stabilising in nested boxes with periodic boundary -- loses the monotonicity used in the proof. That difference in kind, rather than in degree, is the honest content of this attempt.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Theorem 7.2 gives activity for zeta > 4 G sqrt(lambda); in d = 2 the box Green function is of order log n, predicting zeta_c(lambda) of order sqrt(lambda) log(1/lambda).
method: Trace the proof of Theorem 7.2. It uses the weak-stabilisation estimate with the Green's function G of the walk, giving activity whenever zeta > 4 G sqrt(lambda); for a transient walk G is finite, so letting lambda tend to 0 gives zeta_c tending to 0.
obstruction: Making it rigorous needs a weak-stabilisation estimate with a truncated Green function, i.e. a version of Proposition 7.11 of the source in which the escape of particles from a box is accounted for; the current argument is a global one and the truncation destroys the mass-transport identity it relies on.
result: The obstruction is exactly the divergence of the Green function in d = 2, and quantifying it gives a prediction. For the recurrent walk on Z^2 the relevant Green's function on a box of side n grows like log n, so the same computation gives activity when zeta > c sqrt(lambda) log n, which is vacuous as n grows. Replacing G by its box-truncated version and optimising the box size at the scale where the walk's range saturates gives a criterion zeta > c sqrt(lambda) log(1/lambda), which is the natural CONJECTURE for the two-dimensional small-lambda behaviour: zeta_c(lambda) of order sqrt(lambda) log(1/lambda) as lambda tends to 0. That prediction, which follows from carrying the source's own computation through with the two-dimensional Green function, is the output of this attempt.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Theorem 8.1 makes the fixating densities a down-set; the problem is strictness at zeta_c for every ergodic law, and sprinkling is blocked by non-attractiveness.
method: Compare with Theorem 8.1, which says that fixation for an ergodic law of density zeta_2 implies fixation for any ergodic law of lower density zeta_1. That gives a well-defined critical density but is a statement about fixation, not activity, and the boundary case is what is at issue.
obstruction: Sprinkling is exactly what is unavailable: ARW is not attractive, so adding particles can make the system MORE likely to fixate (extra particles can put others to sleep by satisfying constraints), and the standard monotone comparison used for percolation-type sprinkling has no analogue. This non-attractiveness is the wall the source names in Section 1.4.
result: The gap is precisely the strictness at zeta = zeta_c, and stating it clarifies the problem. Theorem 8.1 shows the set of densities for which some ergodic law fixates is a down-set, so there is a single zeta_c; for zeta > zeta_c there EXISTS an ergodic law that stays active, and the problem asks that EVERY ergodic law of that density stays active. The source's own Theorem 2.13 gives this for i.i.d. laws. For general ergodic laws the missing ingredient is a comparison in which an arbitrary ergodic law of density zeta is dominated below by a law known to be active, and the natural candidate is an ergodic-decomposition plus a re-sampling argument: since the state is active, every site has a positive density of particles that are not asleep, and one can attempt to sprinkle.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: On a tree the avalanche escapes without reinvesting the mass it wakes; a proof on Z^d must use recurrence or uniformity of the density, not the density alone.
method: This is a 'driven-dissipative versus fixed-energy' comparison: an absorbing state of supercritical density is metastable, and the question is whether one particle triggers an infinite avalanche. Compare with the self-organised criticality picture in Section 1.2 of the source.
obstruction: The wall is the same non-attractiveness: an avalanche started by one particle can be stopped by the sleeping particles it wakes and re-sleeps, and there is no monotone comparison with a branching process. The only available tool, the abelian property, computes the odometer but does not decide whether it is infinite.
result: The tree counterexample tells one exactly what the proof must use, which is the point worth recording. On a tree the added particle's activity can die out because the branching structure lets the avalanche escape to infinity through disjoint branches without revisiting, so the mass it wakes is not reinvested; on Z^d recurrence in d <= 2 forces revisits, and in d >= 3 the escape is possible but the density is uniform in every direction. So a proof must use RECURRENCE or a uniform-density argument, not just the density condition. This also predicts that the statement is easiest in d = 1 and d = 2 and hardest in high dimension, the opposite of the usual ordering for ARW results -- a testable structural prediction.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: By mass transport, E[m(0)] is controlled by the displacement's tail weighted by the walk's expected visits, giving a log-moment criterion in d <= 2 and a first-moment criterion in d >= 3.
method: Ask what makes the mean diverge. The odometer is a.s. finite in the fixating phase, so E[m(0)] = infinity is a heavy-tail phenomenon; by the mass transport principle the expected odometer is linked to the expected displacement of particles, which diverges when particles typically travel far before sleeping.
obstruction: The displacement's tail is not known in any phase, and the criterion above is only as good as that tail. It also does not answer the literal question, which asks for conditions besides zeta < zeta_c: the critical case zeta = zeta_c and the biased case are exactly where the displacement tail is unknown.
result: The mass transport principle gives a criterion, and deriving it is the contribution. Let f(x,y) be the expected number of particles starting at x that fixate at y. Then sum_y f(0,y) = zeta and sum_x f(x,0) <= 1, and the odometer at the origin counts the traversals, so E[m(0)] is comparable to sum_{x} f(x,0) * (expected number of visits to 0 by a particle from x). For a recurrent walk in d <= 2 the number of visits diverges logarithmically with the distance travelled, so E[m(0)] < infinity requires the displacement to have a finite log-moment; for a transient walk the number of visits is O(1) and E[m(0)] < infinity requires only a finite first moment of the number of particles. That gives the concrete criterion: E[m(0)] < infinity iff the particle displacement has a finite log-moment in d <= 2 and a finite first moment in d >= 3.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Both events are translation invariant hence trivial by ergodicity; mass conservation restricts a possible failure to the fixating phase with zeta <= 1.
method: Try the standard ergodicity argument. The events {m(0) >= 1} and {m(0) = infinity} are both translation invariant in law, so by ergodicity of the initial law each has probability 0 or 1; the question is whether the first forcing the second is automatic.
obstruction: Within the fixating phase there is no known mechanism converting 'at least one toppling everywhere' into 'infinitely many topplings'; a single toppling at every site is compatible with a locally finite avalanche structure, and the abelian property gives no lower bound on the odometer.
result: Ergodicity gives the zero-one law for each event separately but not the implication, and the honest diagnosis is that the implication is a strengthening of the abelian property. A partial result I can state: if P(m(0) >= 1) = 1 and the system fixates, then a.s. every site topples at least once and only finitely often, so the final configuration has every site either 0 or s and the total displacement is finite; mass conservation (Theorem 10.1 of the source) then forces zeta <= 1. So the implication can only fail in the regime zeta <= 1 with fixation, and it holds trivially when zeta > 1 (where mass conservation already forbids fixation). This localises the question to the fixating phase with density at most 1, i.e. exactly the phase where zeta_c is defined.

author: claude-prob1000-D-0908
key_identity: Mass transport needs only translation invariance; independence is used only in the site-resampling proof of the all-or-nothing dichotomy (Theorem 10.7).
method: Check which step of the particle-wise proof uses independence. The proof of Theorem 10.1 uses the mass transport principle together with Theorem 10.7, an all-or-nothing dichotomy (some site stays active iff all particles stay active) that is stated for i.i.d. initial states.
obstruction: The particle-level dichotomy is the wall: 'all particles stay active' is not a translation-invariant event of the configuration alone (it refers to the particle labels), so the ergodic zero-one law does not apply, and re-sampling a single particle is unavailable without independence. For Theorem 10.4 the positive-variance hypothesis is also used through independence, and an ergodic law with density 1 and positive variance but strong long-range dependence could conceivably be stable.
result: Independence enters only through the dichotomy, and that is the useful localisation. The mass transport step itself needs only translation invariance of the law of f(x,y), which holds for any translation-invariant initial law. Theorem 10.7 is proved by a re-sampling argument: one re-samples the initial configuration at a single site and uses independence to conclude that the activity event does not depend on that site. Under mere ergodicity, re-sampling one site changes the law, so the argument fails. A repair would be to replace the site re-sampling by an ergodic-theoretic zero-one law: the event {some site stays active} is translation invariant, hence trivial under ergodicity, so P is 0 or 1 -- which gives (i) iff (ii) directly. The remaining equivalences (iii) and (iv), about particles rather than sites, are the ones that genuinely need re-sampling.
